cna.title: Out-of-bounds read in Zephyr HTTP client debug logging of response header fields

descriptions.value:
The HTTP client's debug helper print_header_field() in subsys/net/lib/http/http_client.c formatted an http_parser data-callback slice with a %s conversion: snprintk(output, len + 1, "%s", str). The parser hands its callbacks a pointer and a length into the caller's receive buffer, and those bytes are not NUL terminated. The size argument of snprintk() bounds only the destination, while the %s conversion measures the source first — lib/os/cbprintf_complete.c uses strlen() when no precision is given, and lib/os/cbprintf_nano.c uses strlen() unconditionally — so the read walks past the end of the header field and past the end of the receive buffer until it finds a zero byte.

The slice reaches the helper from on_url(), on_header_field() and on_header_value(), which the parser invokes on bytes that http_wait_data() read straight off the socket into the application-supplied recv_buf. A malicious or compromised HTTP server, or an attacker able to answer a plaintext request, therefore controls both the header field and the bytes that follow it in the buffer, and can guarantee that no zero byte appears before the buffer ends, forcing the over-read. The in-tree tests/net/lib/http_client suite reproduces the over-read under CONFIG_ASAN=y on an ordinary GET.

The impact is bounded. The whole helper body is compiled only when the HTTP client log module is explicitly set to Debug (CONFIG_NET_HTTP_LOG_LEVEL_DBG=y, which the global CONFIG_LOG_DEFAULT_LEVEL does not set), so default builds are unaffected. No out-of-bounds write occurs and none of the over-read bytes are emitted into the log, so there is no information disclosure; the consequence is an out-of-bounds read that can fault and panic the device where the buffer abuts an unmapped or MPU/MMU-protected region.

The fix copies exactly the len bytes the parser offered with memcpy() and terminates them, instead of relying on a %s conversion (a %.*s precision would not have sufficed, since cbprintf_nano.c measures the source in full before applying it).

cna.title: Flowise before 3.1.4 Cross-Workspace Credential IDOR via node-load-method

descriptions.value: Flowise is a low-code platform for building LLM applications. In versions up to and including 3.1.3, the POST /api/v1/node-load-method/:name endpoint is mounted without any route-level permission check and invokes component loadMethods with an attacker-controlled nodeName, loadMethod, inputs, and credential value. The selected credential is resolved by raw Credential.id via getCredentialData() and decrypted without verifying Credential.workspaceId against the caller's active or shared workspace, unlike other credential read paths which are workspace-scoped. As a result, an authenticated low-privilege user (or workspace API key) in one workspace can supply a credential ID owned by another workspace and cause Flowise to act as a confused deputy, performing third-party provider calls with the victim workspace's credential and returning provider metadata to the attacker. Statically identified affected load methods include Google Drive listFiles, Google Sheets listSpreadsheets, and AWS DynamoDB KV Storage listTables. The raw credential secret itself is not returned to the attacker. This issue is fixed in version 3.1.4.

references.name: VulnCheck Advisory: Flowise before 3.1.4 Cross-Workspace Credential IDOR via node-load-method

cna.title: File Browser 2.5.0 Directory Deletion via Upload Failure Cleanup

references.name: VulnCheck Advisory: File Browser 2.5.0 Directory Deletion via Upload Failure Cleanup

descriptions.value: File Browser versions >= 2.5.0 and <= 2.63.23 contain an incorrect authorization flaw in the direct-upload endpoint (resourcePostHandler in http/resource.go). Unlike the TUS upload handler, the direct-upload handler does not reject a target that is an existing directory; a POST with ?override=true aimed at a directory fails inside writeFile (a directory cannot be opened for writing) and the failure-cleanup path then calls Fs.RemoveAll on the request path, recursively deleting the entire tree. This cleanup is gated by neither the Perm.Delete permission nor the checkDescendants rule walk applied by the delete and patch handlers, so an authenticated non-administrator holding only the default Create and Modify permissions can delete directories they are not authorized to delete, including rule-denied files within them. Deletion remains confined to the user's scope because ScopedFs.RemoveAll still enforces the scope guard. The faulty cleanup was introduced in v2.5.0; no patched version is available.

descriptions.value: A path traversal vulnerability was found in pulpcore. The content upload API accepts a 'file_url' parameter that allows users with file repository privileges to specify a local file URL for Pulp to download and store. A URL scheme validation check uses a string prefix comparison that only rejects URLs beginning with 'file://', but Python's URL parser recognizes the 'file:' scheme without double slashes, creating a mismatch between what is validated and what is dispatched to the file downloader. An authenticated user with low-privilege repository permissions can supply a specially crafted URL using relative path traversal sequences to read any file accessible to the Pulp server process. In deployments that include Pulp Container, successful exploitation allows an attacker to read the container registry token signing private key and forge bearer tokens, granting unauthorized access to all private container repositories in the affected registry.

cna.title: Signed offset bypasses bounds check in simulated EEPROM driver, allowing out-of-bounds kernel memory read and write from user mode

descriptions.value:
The simulated EEPROM driver validated access ranges in eeprom_range_is_valid() (drivers/eeprom/eeprom_simulator.c) with a single test, (offset + len) <= config->size. Because offset is a signed off_t and len an unsigned size_t of the same rank, the addition is evaluated in unsigned arithmetic: a negative offset combined with a compensating len wraps the sum back into the accepted range. eeprom_sim_read() and eeprom_sim_write() then memcpy() through the EEPROM(addr) macro, which is plain pointer arithmetic on the driver's static mock_eeprom array, so the copy addresses memory located before that array.

eeprom_read() and eeprom_write() are __syscall entry points, and their verification handlers in drivers/eeprom/eeprom_handlers.c check only the device object and the caller's own data buffer (K_SYSCALL_MEMORY_READ/K_SYSCALL_MEMORY_WRITE) — the offset argument is passed to the driver unvalidated. With CONFIG_USERSPACE=y, a CONFIG_EEPROM_SIMULATOR device instance, and the device object granted to a user thread (the usage the in-tree tests/drivers/eeprom/api suite exercises from ZTEST_USER threads), an unprivileged thread could supply a negative offset and have the kernel perform the copy on its behalf.

The result is an out-of-bounds read of kernel .bss returned into the caller's buffer and, via the write path, an out-of-bounds write of caller-supplied bytes over kernel memory preceding mock_eeprom. Both the start address and the length of the affected span are attacker-selected, so the primitive is sufficient to corrupt adjacent kernel state and escape the user-mode sandbox. Exposure is limited to builds that instantiate the simulated EEPROM (status = "okay" by default on qemu_x86 and native_sim, otherwise added by a devicetree overlay) together with userspace isolation.

The fix rejects negative offsets and performs the remaining bound check without overflow.

descriptions.value: wasm2c in WebAssembly wabt through 1.0.41 allows sandbox escape in some situations that primarily involve 32-bit platforms, aka a "table flip" attack. It does not check the return value of calloc() in wasm_rt_allocate_funcref_table() (wasm2c/wasm-rt-impl-tableops.inc). When the funcref table allocation fails, table->data is left NULL while table->size keeps the guest-declared element count; thus, bounds checks still pass and table element accesses resolve to absolute memory addresses (i * sizeof(wasm_rt_funcref_t)). This gives arbitrary read and write of host process memory and - via table.get, table.set, and call_indirect - arbitrary code execution, defeating the isolation that wasm2c exists to provide (a full sandbox escape). wasm2c is used as an in-process sandboxing boundary by RLBox and WasmBoxC, including in Firefox, which compiles the Graphite, Hunspell, Ogg, Expat, and Woff2 libraries via wasm2c to contain untrusted font, media, and XML input. Therefore, sandboxing in these applications is potentially affected. Exploitation requires the funcref table allocation to fail, for example under an address-space limit (RLIMIT_AS), on 32-bit hosts, with vm.overcommit_memory=2, or under memory pressure. On 64-bit Linux with default overcommit the allocation succeeds and the defect is not triggered. The wasm2c memory allocator aborts on calloc failure in the same runtime; the table allocator lacks this abort behavior. This was introduced in commit ab9e0b55 (PR #813).

cna.title: Renesas RA SCI UART driver: unacknowledged receive-error interrupt causes a permanent interrupt storm and CPU lockup

descriptions.value:
The Renesas RA SCI UART driver's receive-error ISR, uart_ra_sci_eri_isr() in drivers/serial/uart_renesas_ra_sci.c, acknowledged the error condition only when a Zephyr interrupt-driven callback had already been registered. With CONFIG_UART_INTERRUPT_DRIVEN=y and CONFIG_UART_ASYNC_API=n, if data->user_cb is NULL the ISR body is empty: the SCI error flags (SSR.ORER, SSR.FER, SSR.PER) are left set and the ICU event flag R_ICU->IELSR_b[eri_irq].IR is never cleared, so the interrupt re-pends immediately and the ISR is re-entered without end.

The error interrupt is masked at boot by uart_ra_sci_init(), but FSP's R_SCI_UART_Open() unconditionally re-enables it, and uart_ra_sci_configure() - the back end of the public uart_configure() API, enabled by default via CONFIG_UART_USE_RUNTIME_CONFIGURE - performs a Close()/Open() pair without re-masking it. Any runtime uart_configure() therefore leaves the error interrupt live regardless of whether a callback has been set, as does calling uart_irq_err_enable() on its own. An instance used with the polling API, or the window between uart_configure() and uart_irq_callback_user_data_set(), thus runs with the error interrupt unmasked and no callback registered.

The trigger is an ordinary receive line error - overrun, framing, parity, or a break condition - which is fully determined by the device attached to the serial link. A peer able to assert a break or transmit at a mismatched baud rate produces such an error at will, so a single frame is enough to enter the state.

The impact is availability only: the CPU is captured in the re-entering ISR and never returns to thread context, hanging the entire system until an external reset or hardware watchdog fires. There is no memory corruption or information disclosure. cna.title: Out-of-bounds read in Bluetooth Host periodic advertising report reassembly due to unvalidated report length

descriptions.value:
bt_hci_le_per_adv_report_common() in subsys/bluetooth/host/scan.c handles the HCI_LE_Periodic_Advertising_Report (and _v2) event. It verified that the fixed event header was present and that the controller-declared Data_Length fits the tailroom of the periodic-sync reassembly buffer, but never checked that the event actually carried as many data bytes as evt->length claims. Both reassembly paths — DATA_STATUS_PARTIAL, and DATA_STATUS_COMPLETE while a chain is already in progress — then called net_buf_simple_add_mem(&per_adv_sync->reassembly, buf->data, evt->length), copying up to 255 bytes starting past the end of the event's real payload.

The Data_Length field originates in the HCI controller, so the flaw is reachable in host-only/split builds where the controller is a separate part reached over H4 UART, SPI, USB or an inter-core IPC transport: a malicious, compromised or buggy controller (or an attacker able to inject on that link) can send a report declaring a length larger than the event payload. The generic event dispatcher in subsys/bluetooth/host/hci_core.c only enforces a per-event minimum length and never cross-checks the subevent's internal length field, so nothing else catches it. Builds using Zephyr's own in-image controller are not affected, because the controller always emits a length matching the bytes it appends.

Exploitation additionally requires CONFIG_BT_PER_ADV_SYNC with CONFIG_BT_PER_ADV_SYNC_BUF_SIZE > 0 (the option defaults to 0, which compiles the reassembly block out; LE Audio broadcast-sink and Public Broadcast Profile applications that reassemble fragmented periodic advertising data set it), and an established periodic advertising sync.

The consequence is an out-of-bounds read of adjacent HCI RX-pool memory — including stale contents of previously received HCI events — which is copied into the reassembly buffer and then delivered to every registered bt_le_per_adv_sync_cb.recv listener as if it were received advertising data, so the disclosed memory becomes application-visible and may be forwarded off-device. The write side remains in bounds because the tailroom check uses the same length value, so there is no memory corruption; impact is limited to information disclosure and undefined behaviour on the over-read. The fix drops any report whose declared length exceeds the remaining event payload, matching the guard already present in the extended and legacy advertising report handlers.

cna.title: HTTP::Body versions before 1.24_01 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via regex backtracking on the filename of a multipart upload

solutions.value: Upgrade to HTTP-Body 1.24_01 or later.

descriptions.value:
HTTP::Body versions before 1.24_01 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via regex backtracking on the filename of a multipart upload.

For every file part, the multipart parser finds the suffix of the uploaded filename by matching the default $basename_regexp, qr/[^.]+(\.[^\\\/]+)$/, against the whole basename. A basename made of many dots and ending in a backslash makes the regex backtrack in time quadratic in its length.

A remote attacker can exhaust CPU with one request, as a basename of about 32 KB takes several seconds to match and every file part is matched separately.

workarounds.value: Before passing a hostname to idna, reject any domain that contains a label longer than 63 octets. The DNS limits labels to that length, so legitimate names pass unchanged, and the decoder never runs on the crafted label. The check must run before every call that reaches idna:ulabel/1, including encode/1 and to_ascii/1, because alabel/1 decodes an ASCII xn-- label before checking its length.

descriptions.value:
Inefficient Algorithmic Complexity vulnerability in benoitc idna allows an attacker who controls a hostname passed to the library to exhaust CPU via an over-long xn-- label. idna:ulabel/1 in src/idna.erl hands every ASCII label that starts with xn-- to punycode:decode/1 without applying check_label_length/1, the 63-octet DNS label limit. punycode:decode/1 in src/punycode.erl builds its output with list appends in insert/4, so its cost grows super-linearly with the label length. A label of a few kilobytes keeps a scheduler busy for seconds to minutes before the label is rejected as invalid punycode.

Every decode entry point reaches this path: decode/1, decode/2, to_unicode/1 and from_ascii/1. The encode path reaches it as well, because alabel/1 calls ulabel/1 on an ASCII xn-- label before its own length check, so encode/1, encode/2 and to_ascii/1 are affected for such input.

This issue affects idna: from 0.5.0 before 8.0.0.

x_technicalAnalysis.value:
1. Label dispatch. idna:decode/2 in src/idna.erl lowercases the domain, splits it into labels and passes each one to ulabel/1. For an all-ASCII label that starts with xn--, ulabel/1 strips the prefix and calls punycode:decode/1 on the remainder. No length check runs before that call. check_label_length/1, which rejects labels longer than 63 octets, is only called from alabel/1, and there only after alabel/1 has itself called ulabel/1 on an ASCII label.

2. Super-linear decoding. punycode:decode/1 in src/punycode.erl decodes one code point per delta and places it into the output with insert/4. insert/4 walks to the insertion index by rebuilding the head with Head ++ [C] on every step and then appends the tail with another ++. Each insertion therefore costs time quadratic in the insertion index, and the total work grows roughly with the cube of the label length. The reporter measured about an 8x increase in running time per doubling of the label.

3. Work before rejection. The crafted label is not valid punycode and the call eventually exits with an error, but only after the decoder has processed the whole label. The ?MAX overflow guards in punycode:decode/1 cover the RFC 3492 integer overflow class and do not bound the running time.

4. Entry points. decode/1, decode/2, to_unicode/1 and from_ascii/1 reach ulabel/1 in every affected release. From 6.0.0, alabel/1 calls ulabel/1 on any ASCII label that starts with xn-- before check_label_length/1, so encode/1, encode/2, to_ascii/1 and utf8_to_ascii/1 reach the decoder for such input as well.

**1. Label dispatch.** `idna:decode/2` in `src/idna.erl` lowercases the domain, splits it into labels and passes each one to `ulabel/1`. For an all-ASCII label that starts with `xn--`, `ulabel/1` strips the prefix and calls `punycode:decode/1` on the remainder. No length check runs before that call. `check_label_length/1`, which rejects labels longer than 63 octets, is only called from `alabel/1`, and there only after `alabel/1` has itself called `ulabel/1` on an ASCII label.

**2. Super-linear decoding.** `punycode:decode/1` in `src/punycode.erl` decodes one code point per delta and places it into the output with `insert/4`. `insert/4` walks to the insertion index by rebuilding the head with `Head ++ [C]` on every step and then appends the tail with another `++`. Each insertion therefore costs time quadratic in the insertion index, and the total work grows roughly with the cube of the label length. The reporter measured about an 8x increase in running time per doubling of the label.

**3. Work before rejection.** The crafted label is not valid punycode and the call eventually exits with an error, but only after the decoder has processed the whole label. The `?MAX` overflow guards in `punycode:decode/1` cover the RFC 3492 integer overflow class and do not bound the running time.

**4. Entry points.** `decode/1`, `decode/2`, `to_unicode/1` and `from_ascii/1` reach `ulabel/1` in every affected release. From 6.0.0, `alabel/1` calls `ulabel/1` on any ASCII label that starts with `xn--` before `check_label_length/1`, so `encode/1`, `encode/2`, `to_ascii/1` and `utf8_to_ascii/1` reach the decoder for such input as well.

cna.title: Typecho before 1.3.1-rc SSRF via DNS Rebinding in XML-RPC pingback.ping

references.name: VulnCheck Advisory: Typecho before 1.3.1-rc SSRF via DNS Rebinding in XML-RPC pingback.ping

descriptions.value: Typecho before 1.3.1-rc contains a server-side request forgery vulnerability in the XML-RPC pingback.ping method where checkSafeHost() validates a hostname's resolved IP once but the subsequent outbound request performs an independent DNS resolution, creating a TOCTOU window exploitable via DNS rebinding. An unauthenticated attacker can configure a domain to return a benign IP at validation time and an internal address (loopback, RFC1918, or cloud metadata IP) at request time, causing the server to issue blind SSRF requests to arbitrary internal hosts and ports.

credits.value: Red Hat would like to thank Dongju Lee (@br0nzu) for reporting this issue.

workarounds.value: Mitigation for this issue is either not available or the currently available options do not meet the Red Hat Product Security criteria comprising ease of use and deployment, applicability to widespread installation base, or stability.

descriptions.value: A flaw was found in the client registration component of Keycloak, an open-source identity and access management solution. When a vault provider is used to store sensitive information, an authenticated client owner can use a specially crafted reference to trick the system into revealing secrets. By updating a client secret to point to a vault entry and then requesting the client configuration, the owner can see the secret value in plain text. This could lead to the exposure of sensitive credentials that the user should not be able to access.

descriptions.value: The Dynific Addons for Elementor (formerly Anywhere Elementor) WordPress plugin before 1.3.1 does not escape the post title before outputting it in a quoted HTML attribute in one of its Elementor widgets, allowing authenticated users with the Author role to publish a post whose title executes as script in the session of anyone, including an administrator, who views it, resulting in Stored Cross-Site Scripting.

cna.title: @fastify/secure-session vulnerable to signature verification bypass via cookie signature removal

descriptions.value: @fastify/secure-session is a session plugin for Fastify that stores an encrypted session in a cookie. In versions 7.5.0 through 8.4.1, when the plugin is configured with the signed cookie option, it calls the cookie unsign routine but, when the signature check reports the value as invalid, still passes the original cookie value to the session decoder, so a session whose signature did not validate is decrypted anyway. The practical effect appears when an application supplies the cookie signing secret independently of the session encryption key and rotates only the signing secret to retire existing sessions while keeping the encryption key active, because a holder of an old session cookie can strip the now obsolete signature and keep using the session. The attacker must already possess an unexpired encrypted session cookie and needs neither secret, and cannot forge session data, extend expiry, or survive rotation of the encryption key. The issue is fixed in @fastify/secure-session 8.4.2, which no longer decodes the session when the signed cookie option is set and the signature check fails, and users should upgrade to 8.4.2 or later. As a workaround, rotate the session encryption key rather than relying on rotation of the cookie signing secret alone.

cna.title: User-controlled Duo host permits authenticated SSRF in Psono Server

descriptions.value: An authenticated user could induce outbound HTTPS connections to selected hosts, use response differences as an internal reachability oracle, and occupy workers through connection timeouts.

solutions.value: Upgrade to Psono Server 7.2.4 or later.

supportingMedia.value: Upgrade to Psono Server 7.2.4 or later.

descriptions.value: Psono Server CE && EE versions 0.1.0 through 7.2.3 accepted a user-controlled host when configuring a personal Duo device and passed it to the Duo client without an allowlist or explicit timeout. An authenticated remote attacker could cause the server to connect to selected hosts over HTTPS on port 443 and distinguish failure modes, providing an internal DNS and service-reachability oracle. Connections still required TLS certificate validation, and the flaw did not provide arbitrary protocol or port access. Unresponsive targets could also occupy a server worker until the operating-system timeout.

cna.title: Gitea private issue disclosure through issue dependency timeline events

references.name: Fix backport to release/v28: go-gitea/gitea pull request #40085
Related fix (hidden dependency attachments, 28.2.0): go-gitea/gitea pull request #39839
Related fix backport to release/v28 (28.2.0): go-gitea/gitea pull request #39847

descriptions.value: The issue timeline API and the web issue page hid cross-reference events that point at issues the reader cannot access, but not "dependency added" and "dependency removed" events. When a readable issue had been linked as a dependency to an issue in a repository the reader cannot access, for example a private repository, any reader of the first issue, including anonymous users of a public repository, received the linked issue's current title, body, state, labels, poster and attachment names through the API, and its repository, number and title on the web page. Creating the link requires access to both issues; comments and attachment downloads of the linked issue stayed protected. Dependency events are now filtered with the same read permission check; a related exposure of unlinked attachment metadata through hidden dependency placeholders was already fixed in 28.2.0.

descriptions.value: The repositories, stars and watching tabs of user profiles and the repository list of organization home pages included private repositories for every signed-in request without checking whether the request used a personal access token restricted to public resources (`public-only`). A holder of such a token could list the private repositories visible to the token's owner, and that user's stars and watches of private repositories. workarounds.value: Remove the user parameter from the callback parameters before you pass them to Assent.Strategy.Apple.callback/2, for example with Map.delete(params, "user"). The user's name is then unavailable, because Apple delivers it only through this parameter.

Remove the `user` parameter from the callback parameters before you pass them to `Assent.Strategy.Apple.callback/2`, for example with `Map.delete(params, "user")`. The user's name is then unavailable, because Apple delivers it only through this parameter.

descriptions.value:
Acceptance of Extraneous Untrusted Data With Trusted Data vulnerability in the Sign in with Apple strategy in pow-auth Assent allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to impersonate another user via the user parameter of the authorization callback.

Apple posts the user's name to the callback endpoint in a user form parameter that the browser submits and the client controls. Assent.Strategy.Apple.callback/2 in lib/assent/strategies/apple.ex decodes that parameter, and fetch_user/2 merges it over the claims of the verified ID token, so the unverified map wins. An attacker who completes a Sign in with Apple login with their own Apple ID and edits the user parameter can replace sub, email, and any other claim. Applications that look up, link, or authorize accounts by the returned subject or email then act on the attacker's values.

This issue affects assent: from 0.1.25 before 0.3.2.

x_proofOfConcept.value:
* Start the Sign in with Apple flow of an application that uses Assent.Strategy.Apple.
* Authenticate at Apple with an Apple ID the attacker controls.
* Intercept the form_post request to the application's callback URL and set the user parameter to a JSON object that carries the victim's values, such as {"sub": "<victim subject>", "email": "victim@example.com"}.
* The application calls Assent.Strategy.Apple.callback/2. It validates the attacker's ID token and returns a user map whose sub and email are the victim's values, with email_verified set to true.

1. Start the Sign in with Apple flow of an application that uses `Assent.Strategy.Apple`.
2. Authenticate at Apple with an Apple ID the attacker controls.
3. Intercept the `form_post` request to the application's callback URL and set the `user` parameter to a JSON object that carries the victim's values, such as `{"sub": "<victim subject>", "email": "victim@example.com"}`.
4. The application calls `Assent.Strategy.Apple.callback/2`. It validates the attacker's ID token and returns a user map whose `sub` and `email` are the victim's values, with `email_verified` set to true.

x_technicalAnalysis.value:
1. Unverified input. Apple's form_post response mode delivers code, id_token, state, and on the first authorization a user parameter that holds a JSON object with the user's name and email. The browser submits this parameter and Apple does not sign it, so the client controls its content.

2. Merge over verified claims. Assent.Strategy.Apple.callback/2 decodes the user parameter with Helpers.decode_json/2 and stores the map in the config under :user. After Assent.Strategy.OIDC.fetch_user/2 has validated the ID token, Assent.Strategy.Apple.fetch_user/2 calls Map.merge/2 with the verified claims first and the decoded parameter second. Keys from the parameter overwrite keys from the token, including sub and email.

3. Result. normalize/2 reads sub and email from the merged map and sets email_verified to true, so the application receives attacker-chosen identity fields marked as verified.

4. Fix. Version 0.3.2 ignores the parameter by default. With include_unverified_name: true, only given_name and family_name are taken from it, and the verified claims are merged over them.

**1. Unverified input.** Apple's `form_post` response mode delivers `code`, `id_token`, `state`, and on the first authorization a `user` parameter that holds a JSON object with the user's name and email. The browser submits this parameter and Apple does not sign it, so the client controls its content.

**2. Merge over verified claims.** `Assent.Strategy.Apple.callback/2` decodes the `user` parameter with `Helpers.decode_json/2` and stores the map in the config under `:user`. After `Assent.Strategy.OIDC.fetch_user/2` has validated the ID token, `Assent.Strategy.Apple.fetch_user/2` calls `Map.merge/2` with the verified claims first and the decoded parameter second. Keys from the parameter overwrite keys from the token, including `sub` and `email`.

**3. Result.** `normalize/2` reads `sub` and `email` from the merged map and sets `email_verified` to true, so the application receives attacker-chosen identity fields marked as verified.

**4. Fix.** Version 0.3.2 ignores the parameter by default. With `include_unverified_name: true`, only `given_name` and `family_name` are taken from it, and the verified claims are merged over them.

descriptions.value: Janus WebRTC Server 1.2.3 through 1.4.0 is vulnerable to Directory Traversal. The application accepts a caller supplied media path when an ondemand stream is created. The path is validated only by checking whether it contains one of the audio extensions and is then passed to the file source which opens it. No canonicalization is performed and no directory allowlist is enforced, so an unauthenticated caller can make the server open an arbitrary local file and use it as a media source, with the content delivered to viewers as RTP audio.

references.name: VulnCheck Advisory: Electrum before 4.7.2 Nostr Wallet Connect Plugin Daily Spending Limit Bypass

descriptions.value: Electrum before 4.7.2 contains a spending limit bypass vulnerability in the Nostr Wallet Connect plugin that allows malicious NWC clients to exceed daily_limit_sat by exploiting non-atomic budget checks and millisatoshi truncation. Attackers can send concurrent pay_invoice requests that pass budget_allows_spend() before add_to_budget() runs, or repeatedly pay msat amounts that are floored to whole satoshis, to drain funds beyond the limit.

descriptions.value:
Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting') vulnerability in phoenixframework phoenix_html allows an attacker who controls attribute names to inject attributes and script into rendered HTML via Phoenix.HTML.attributes_escape/1.

attributes_escape/1 in lib/phoenix_html.ex escapes attribute values but not attribute names. key_escape/1 passes a binary key through html_escape, which neutralizes quotes and angle brackets but not whitespace, so a key such as x onmouseover ends the attribute and starts a new one. An atom key is only dasherized, so any character passes, including quotes and >. Nested data, aria and phx keys take the same paths. An application is affected when it builds attribute keys from untrusted input and renders them through HEEx <tag {@attrs}>, content_tag/3, or a direct call. Before 3.0.0 the same code lived in Phoenix.HTML.Tag.

This issue affects phoenix_html: from 1.0.0 before 3.3.5 and from 4.0.0 before 4.4.0.

x_technicalAnalysis.value:
1. Attribute rendering. Phoenix.HTML.attributes_escape/1 walks the key-value pairs through build_attrs/1 and nested_attrs/3 and emits each as key_escape(k)="attr_escape(v)". Values are escaped. Names are not checked against the HTML attribute-name grammar.

2. Binary names. key_escape/1 sends a binary through Phoenix.HTML.Engine.html_escape/1, which replaces &, <, >, " and '. Whitespace passes. HTML uses whitespace to separate attributes, so %{"x onmouseover" => "alert(1)"} renders  x onmouseover="alert(1)": a harmless x attribute followed by an attacker-chosen event handler.

3. Atom names. key_escape/1 converts an atom with Atom.to_string/1 and replaces _ with -. Nothing is escaped, so [{:"x\" onclick=\"alert(1)", "y"}] renders  x" onclick="alert(1)="y" and aria: [{:"x\"><script>", "y"}] renders  aria-x"><script>="y", which leaves the tag entirely. This path needs the application to create atoms from untrusted input, for example Jason.decode!(body, keys: :atoms) or String.to_atom/1 on a parameter.

4. Reachability. HEEx compiles <div {@attrs}> to a call to Phoenix.HTML.attributes_escape/1 through Phoenix.LiveView.HTMLEngine and Phoenix.LiveView.TagEngine. tag/2 and content_tag/3 in Phoenix.HTML.Tag (phoenix_html 1.x to 3.x) and in PhoenixHTMLHelpers.Tag (4.x) render attributes the same way. Versions before 3.0.0 emitted the dasherized name without any escaping at all.

**1. Attribute rendering.** `Phoenix.HTML.attributes_escape/1` walks the key-value pairs through `build_attrs/1` and `nested_attrs/3` and emits each as `key_escape(k)="attr_escape(v)"`. Values are escaped. Names are not checked against the HTML attribute-name grammar.

**2. Binary names.** `key_escape/1` sends a binary through `Phoenix.HTML.Engine.html_escape/1`, which replaces `&`, `<`, `>`, `"` and `'`. Whitespace passes. HTML uses whitespace to separate attributes, so `%{"x onmouseover" => "alert(1)"}` renders ` x onmouseover="alert(1)"`: a harmless `x` attribute followed by an attacker-chosen event handler.

**3. Atom names.** `key_escape/1` converts an atom with `Atom.to_string/1` and replaces `_` with `-`. Nothing is escaped, so `[{:"x\" onclick=\"alert(1)", "y"}]` renders ` x" onclick="alert(1)="y"` and `aria: [{:"x\"><script>", "y"}]` renders ` aria-x"><script>="y"`, which leaves the tag entirely. This path needs the application to create atoms from untrusted input, for example `Jason.decode!(body, keys: :atoms)` or `String.to_atom/1` on a parameter.

**4. Reachability.** HEEx compiles `<div {@attrs}>` to a call to `Phoenix.HTML.attributes_escape/1` through `Phoenix.LiveView.HTMLEngine` and `Phoenix.LiveView.TagEngine`. `tag/2` and `content_tag/3` in `Phoenix.HTML.Tag` (phoenix_html 1.x to 3.x) and in `PhoenixHTMLHelpers.Tag` (4.x) render attributes the same way. Versions before 3.0.0 emitted the dasherized name without any escaping at all.

cna.title: @fastify/multipart vulnerable to Denial of Service via a malformed upload hanging delayed file consumers

descriptions.value: @fastify/multipart is the multipart form-data and file upload plugin for the Fastify web framework. In versions 5.3.0 through 10.1.6, the plugin does not propagate a parser error to the file stream when a request body ends inside a file part with no closing boundary, even though the Content-Length is complete, the client does not abort, and no file size limit is exceeded. The plugin destroys the in-progress file stream without an error, so a handler that iterates the request parts and performs asynchronous work before consuming the file attaches to a stream that never emits an error or end event, and the request never responds while the connection stays open. An unauthenticated remote client can repeat these malformed uploads against such a route to accumulate pending connections and exhaust server resources, so the impact is availability only and exploitation depends on the application using a delayed file consumer. The issue is fixed in @fastify/multipart 10.1.7, where the parser error is propagated to the file stream so a delayed consumer settles with an error instead of hanging, and users should upgrade to 10.1.7 or later. There is no workaround other than upgrading.

cna.title: URL prefix handling permits API key read-scope bypass in Psono Server

descriptions.value: A write-only API key could read encrypted secret records through the bulk-secret-read endpoint despite having its read scope disabled.

solutions.value: Upgrade to Psono Server 7.2.4 or later.

supportingMedia.value: Upgrade to Psono Server 7.2.4 or later.

descriptions.value: Psono Server CE && EE versions 4.0.33 through 7.2.3 compared the request path for the bulk-secret-read endpoint with a hard-coded unprefixed path. In deployments configured with URL_PREFIX, the comparison failed and the POST request was authorized using write scope instead of read scope. An authenticated remote attacker with an unusual read-disabled, write-enabled API key could therefore retrieve encrypted secret data and nonces through the prefixed bulk-secret-read endpoint despite lacking read permission. The default configuration without URL_PREFIX was not affected.

descriptions.value:
Improper Check for Unusual or Exceptional Conditions vulnerability in the pattern and patternProperties keywords in lud jsv allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to bypass schema validation via a string that matches a schema regex only after heavy backtracking. JSV.Helpers.RegexExt.bounded_match?/2 runs schema regexes with a backtracking budget but calls :re.run/3 without :report_errors, so a match that exhausts the budget returns the same :nomatch as a real non-match. A key that matches a patternProperties regex is then checked against additionalProperties or not at all, and a string that matches a not subschema with a pattern is accepted. Before the budget existed, Regex.match?/2 failed the same way at Erlang's default match limit.

Only schemas whose regex explores a catastrophic branch before the branch that matches are affected. The attacker controls the data, not the schema, and linear patterns never exhaust the budget.

This issue affects jsv: from 0.1.0 before 0.26.2.

* Build a schema with patternProperties mapping the regex ^(?:(a+)+b|a+!)$ to {"type": "integer"}.
* Submit an object whose only key is twenty a characters followed by ! and whose value is the string not an int. The key matches the regex through its second alternative, but PCRE exhausts the 11,050-step budget in the first alternative.

* Build a second schema {"not": {"pattern": "^(?:(a+)+b|a+!)$"}} and submit the same string. JSV.validate/2 returns :ok although the string matches the denied pattern.

x_technicalAnalysis.value:
1. Bounded matching. JSV.Helpers.RegexExt.bounded_match?/2 in lib/jsv/helpers/regex_ext.ex runs each schema regex through :re.run/3 with match_limit and match_limit_recursion set to 10_000 + 50 * byte_size(subject), capped at 10,000,000. The call omits :report_errors, so PCRE's match_limit error is returned as :nomatch. The function compares the result to :match and returns false for a genuine non-match and for an exhausted budget alike.

2. Keyword evaluation. JSV.Vocabulary.V202012.Validation.validate_keyword/3 uses the result for pattern, and JSV.Vocabulary.V202012.Applicator uses it to decide which patternProperties subschemas apply to each key. The draft 7 vocabulary delegates to the same modules. A false from an exhausted budget therefore means a pattern keyword fails and a patternProperties subschema is skipped.

3. Inversion by combinators. Under not, anyOf, oneOf, if and contains, a failing subschema can make the parent succeed, so a false non-match under not accepts a string the deny-list should reject. Under patternProperties the skipped subschema means the value is checked against additionalProperties or nothing.

4. History. Before the budget was introduced, the same keywords called Regex.match?/2, which also returns false on Erlang's default limit of 10,000,000 steps. The budget lowered the input size needed from about 25 bytes to about 20 bytes for the advisory's pattern.

cna.title: @fastify/reply-from vulnerable to path traversal via backslash dot-segment prefix escape

descriptions.value: @fastify/reply-from is a Fastify plugin that forwards requests to an upstream HTTP server. In versions up to and including 12.8.0, the plugin validated proxy paths against forward-slash dot-segments only and then built the target with the WHATWG URL parser, which normalizes a backslash and its percent-encoded form to a forward slash on the http, https, ws, and wss schemes. A path that uses backslash dot-segments therefore bypasses the traversal check and resolves to a different upstream path, so an application that scopes proxying to an upstream prefix, or relies on route guards in front of the forwarding call, can have an unauthenticated request escape the intended prefix and reach other upstream endpoints. The resulting access to unintended upstream resources is primarily a confidentiality impact with limited integrity impact. The issue is fixed in @fastify/reply-from 12.8.1, where the path is normalized and any segment resolving to a single or double dot, along with control characters and ambiguous whitespace, is rejected before the URL is constructed, and users should upgrade to 12.8.1 or later. There is no workaround other than upgrading.

cna.title: Keycloak-services: keycloak-services: saml redirect binding signature bypass via percent-encoded parameter names

credits.value: Red Hat would like to thank Mayssen Aidoudi (Think-it GmbH) for reporting this issue.

workarounds.value:
Mitigation for this issue is either not available or the currently available options do not meet the Red Hat Product Security criteria comprising ease of use and deployment, applicability to widespread installation base, or stability.

--- CME Mitigation Guidance (2026-11-06) ---
Disclaimer: The following mitigation solutions are provided as a courtesy, pending the application of an official patch. This content was generated utilizing AI tools in conjunction with data from https://cmetaxonomy.org. Customers are advised to independently evaluate and test these temporary mitigations within their own infrastructure.

The highest-value action is to align query parameter parsing between signature verification and request processing in Keycloak's SAML HTTP-Redirect binding so percent-encoded parameter names cannot evade signature checks: upgrade to the fixed Rhbk/Keycloak Rhel/Keycloak Services builds, which eliminates the parsing discrepancy between raw query parameter signature verification and decoded parameter processing in the SAML redirect binding, closing crafted HTTP GET request containing a percent-encoded unsigned SAML parameter placed before a legitimately signed parameter. Until patched, this is a concern on Keycloak instances configured to use SAML HTTP-Redirect binding for federated identity, so Audit and restrict account registration on external Identity Providers to prevent attackers from capturing legitimately signed redirect-binding messages. These controls limit blast radius and contain exploitation, but they do not fix the underlying SAML parameter parsing discrepancy signature bypass — apply the upstream patch to fully remediate.

descriptions.value: A flaw was found in the SAML HTTP-Redirect binding implementation of Keycloak. The issue occurs because the server processes percent-encoded parameter names (like %53AMLResponse) while the signature verification logic only checks literal parameter names. An attacker can use this discrepancy to provide a crafted, unsigned SAML message that the server processes instead of a legitimately signed one, leading to full account takeover of federated users.

descriptions.value: A flaw was found in the JWT Authorization Grant implementation of the keycloak-services component. descriptions.value: The OCI registry's cross-repository blob mount checked the target package against the token's `public-only` restriction, but checked the source blob only against the full account permissions of the token owner. A `public-only` token with `write:package` scope, whose owner can read a private package and write to a public package namespace, could mount a blob of the private package into the public package. The private blob, such as a container layer, could then be downloaded by anyone through the public package.

cna.title: File-transfer type confusion permits unauthorized repository writes in Psono Server

descriptions.value: A user with read-only file access could upload objects and append chunks in the file owner's external repository, affecting storage integrity and availability.

solutions.value: Upgrade to Psono Server 7.2.4 or later.

supportingMedia.value: Upgrade to Psono Server 7.2.4 or later.

descriptions.value: Psono Server (CE & EE) versions 1.0.0 through 7.2.3 did not enforce the direction of file-transfer credentials on file-repository operations. An authenticated remote attacker with read-only access to a file could present a download transfer to the upload endpoint, obtain a signed upload URL for an attacker-selected object key, and append a chunk to the owner's file. Exploitation could upload or overwrite repository objects and consume storage, subject to transfer size, chunk-count, and lifetime limits.

cna.title: HTTP::Body versions before 1.24_01 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via unbounded buffering of chunked request bodies

solutions.value: Upgrade to HTTP-Body 1.24_01 or later.

descriptions.value:
HTTP::Body versions before 1.24_01 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via unbounded buffering of chunked request bodies.

In chunked mode, used when no content length is given, add() holds each chunk in memory until all of it has arrived. A line that is not a chunk-size line, a size line without CRLF, or a size too large to fit an integer leaves the parser waiting forever, and every later add() grows the buffer.

A remote attacker can exhaust memory in applications that pass chunked request bodies to HTTP::Body.

descriptions.value: A holder of a certificate for f*.example.net from a CA the client trusts can impersonate any host named f.<label>.example.net to a client that relies on ssl_verify_fun alone for hostname verification, and read or alter the traffic of that connection.

supportingMedia.value: A holder of a certificate for f*.example.net from a CA the client trusts can impersonate any host named f.<label>.example.net to a client that relies on ssl_verify_fun alone for hostname verification, and read or alter the traffic of that connection.

A holder of a certificate for `f*.example.net` from a CA the client trusts can impersonate any host named `f.<label>.example.net` to a client that relies on ssl_verify_fun alone for hostname verification, and read or alter the traffic of that connection.

references.name: ssl_verify_fun: partial-label wildcard certificate matches hostnames across a label boundary
Do not let partial-label wildcards match across label boundaries (ssl_verify_fun.erl pull request #33)

workarounds.value: On Erlang/OTP 21 or later, keep server_name_indication set to the target hostname and pass {customize_hostname_check, [{match_fun, public_key:pkix_verify_hostname_match_fun(https)}]} in the ssl options. The hostname check in ssl then rejects the mismatch before ssl_verify_fun runs, and legitimate wildcard certificates continue to match. hackney and tls_certificate_check already set both options.

The hostname check in `ssl` then rejects the mismatch before ssl_verify_fun runs, and legitimate wildcard certificates continue to match. hackney and tls_certificate_check already set both options.

descriptions.value:
Improper Validation of Certificate with Host Mismatch vulnerability in deadtrickster ssl_verify_fun allows an adversary in the middle to impersonate a TLS peer via a certificate that carries a partial-label wildcard. try_match_wildcard/4 in src/ssl_verify_hostname.erl anchors only the text before and after the * of an identifier such as f*.example.net, so the wildcard also consumes dots and the certificate is accepted for f.evil.example.net. RFC 6125 confines a wildcard to the left-most label. The same matcher lets *.168.1.1 match the IP literal 192.168.1.1. Whole-label wildcards are matched correctly.

Erlang/OTP 20.0 and later check the hostname in ssl before a user verify_fun sees valid_peer, so a client that keeps server_name_indication set rejects the mismatch regardless. Exposed are clients that disable SNI, servers that verify client certificate hostnames with this library, and direct callers of verify_cert_hostname/2.

This issue affects ssl_verify_fun: from 1.0.1 before 1.1.8.

RFC 6125 confines a wildcard to the left-most label. The same matcher lets `*.168.1.1` match the IP literal `192.168.1.1`. Whole-label wildcards are matched correctly.

Exposed are clients that disable SNI, servers that verify client certificate hostnames with this library, and direct callers of `verify_cert_hostname/2`.

This issue affects ssl_verify_fun: from 1.0.1 before 1.1.8.

descriptions.description: CWE-297 Improper Validation of Certificate with Host Mismatch

configurations.value: ssl_verify_fun decides the outcome only where it is the sole hostname check. Erlang/OTP 20.0 and later verify the hostname in ssl before the user verify_fun is called with valid_peer, as long as server_name_indication is a hostname or the connection was upgraded from a socket. A deployment is exposed when it sets {server_name_indication, disable}, when a TLS server uses ssl_verify_hostname:verify_fun/3 to verify client certificates, when it calls ssl_verify_hostname:verify_cert_hostname/2 directly, or when it runs Erlang/OTP older than 20.0. The attacker also needs a certificate with a partial-label wildcard from a CA the client trusts, which the CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements do not allow, so the realistic exposure is private PKI.

x_proofOfConcept.value:
* Issue a leaf certificate whose only subjectAltName entry is dNSName f*.example.net, for example with public_key:pkix_test_data/1, and decode it with public_key:pkix_decode_cert(Der, otp).
* Call ssl_verify_hostname:verify_cert_hostname(Cert, "foo.example.net"). It returns {valid, "foo.example.net"}, as expected.
* Call ssl_verify_hostname:verify_cert_hostname(Cert, "f.evil.example.net"). It returns {valid, "f.evil.example.net"} although the hostname spans two labels where the wildcard sits.
* Call ssl_verify_hostname:verify_cert_hostname(Cert, "a.b.example.net") as a control. It returns {fail, unable_to_match_altnames}.
* For the IP-literal variant, issue a leaf with dNSName *.168.1.1 and call verify_cert_hostname(Cert, "192.168.1.1"). It returns {valid, "192.168.1.1"}.
* To observe the full TLS path, serve the first certificate from ssl:listen/2 and connect with {verify, verify_peer}, the CA in cacerts, {verify_fun, {fun ssl_verify_hostname:verify_fun/3, [{check_hostname, "f.evil.example.net"}]}} and {server_name_indication, disable}. The handshake succeeds. With {server_name_indication, "f.evil.example.net"} instead, OTP 20.0 or later rejects the certificate with hostname_check_failed before ssl_verify_fun runs.

2. Call `ssl_verify_hostname:verify_cert_hostname(Cert, "foo.example.net")`. It returns `{valid, "foo.example.net"}`, as expected.
3. Call `ssl_verify_hostname:verify_cert_hostname(Cert, "f.evil.example.net")`. It returns `{valid, "f.evil.example.net"}` although the hostname spans two labels where the wildcard sits.
4. Call `ssl_verify_hostname:verify_cert_hostname(Cert, "a.b.example.net")` as a control. It returns `{fail, unable_to_match_altnames}`.
5. For the IP-literal variant, issue a leaf with `dNSName` `*.168.1.1` and call `verify_cert_hostname(Cert, "192.168.1.1")`. It returns `{valid, "192.168.1.1"}`.
6. To observe the full TLS path, serve the first certificate from `ssl:listen/2` and connect with `{verify, verify_peer}`, the CA in `cacerts`, `{verify_fun, {fun ssl_verify_hostname:verify_fun/3, [{check_hostname, "f.evil.example.net"}]}}` and `{server_name_indication, disable}`. The handshake succeeds. With `{server_name_indication, "f.evil.example.net"}` instead, OTP 20.0 or later rejects the certificate with `hostname_check_failed` before ssl_verify_fun runs.

x_technicalAnalysis.value:
1. Identifier parsing. ssl_verify_hostname:try_match_hostname/2 strips trailing dots, tries an exact case-insensitive match, and otherwise calls parse_and_validate_wildcard_identifier/2. That function accepts an identifier with one * in the left-most label and at least two labels after it, and classifies it as SingleCharW when the label is exactly *.

2. Whole-label wildcard, correct. For *.example.net the matcher compares the text after the * with the hostname from its first dot onward, so a.b.example.net fails because .b.example.net differs from .example.net.

3. Partial-label wildcard, incorrect. For f*.example.net the SingleCharW branch is skipped. try_match_wildcard/4 then checks only that the hostname ends with .example.net and starts with f. Nothing checks the span consumed by the *, so f.evil.example.net and f.a.b.example.net pass. RFC 6125 section 6.4.3 limits a wildcard to the left-most label. The wildcard_not_in_a_label/2 guard only rejects internationalized xn-- labels and does not help.

4. IP literals. The reference identifier is treated as a DNS name whatever its shape, so verify_cert_hostname/2 with hostname 192.168.1.1 matches a dNSName of *.168.1.1 through the whole-label branch. RFC 6125 does not apply wildcard matching to IP addresses, and OTP's ssl converts an IP-literal string to an {ip, ...} reference that only matches iPAddress entries.

5. Interaction with Erlang/OTP. When ssl_verify_hostname:verify_fun/3 is used as verify_fun, OTP 20.0 and later call ssl_certificate:validate/4 for valid_peer before the user fun. In the client role with server_name_indication set to a hostname, or with a peer IP from a socket upgrade, OTP runs public_key:pkix_verify_hostname/3 and hands the user fun {bad_cert, hostname_check_failed} instead of valid_peer, which ssl_verify_fun turns into {fail, ...}. OTP's default match function allows no wildcards, and its https match function (public_key:pkix_verify_hostname_match_fun/1) splits both names on dots and matches the wildcard within the first label only. The ssl_verify_fun result therefore decides the outcome only with {server_name_indication, disable}, in the server role, on direct calls to verify_cert_hostname/2, or on OTP older than 20.0.

cna.title: 389-ds-base: 389-ds-base: null pointer dereference via modifydn using an attribute's schema alias name causes denial of service

credits.value: Red Hat would like to thank Chad Sikorra for reporting this issue.

workarounds.value: Administrators should review custom access control instructions (ACIs) and avoid granting the ModifyDN (rename) right to non-administrative principals unless specifically required. Restricting this right reduces exposure to this issue until a fixed package is available. Neither 389-ds-base's own default ACI templates nor Red Hat Identity Management (IdM/FreeIPA)'s default ACIs grant this right to non-administrative users, so deployments that have not customized their ACIs are not exposed.

descriptions.value: A NULL pointer dereference flaw was found in 389-ds-base. This flaw occurs when a ModifyDN (rename) operation uses an attribute's schema alias name (such as "commonName") instead of its canonical name (such as "cn") as the new relative distinguished name. An authenticated attacker with the ModifyDN (rename) permission on the affected entry can use this flaw to crash the directory server, causing a denial of service.

cna.title: @fastify/session vulnerable to session revocation bypass via a logout race condition

descriptions.value: @fastify/session is a session plugin for Fastify. In all releases before 11.1.6, with the default rolling session behavior, a request that restored a session before a logout could save its own copy after another request had completed the session destroy call, recreating the destroyed session identifier with its authenticated data. An attacker who already holds a victim's valid signed session cookie and keeps a request in flight across the logout can replay that cookie to restore the session after it was meant to be revoked, without any cookie theft or signature forgery. The issue is fixed in @fastify/session 11.1.6, which adds a per session generation marker and a conditional store write so a session restored before a logout or regeneration cannot recreate or overwrite the current entry, and users should upgrade to 11.1.6 or later. There is no workaround, and custom session stores must implement the new conditional write.

cna.title: SPL Injection through Finding Exclusion Rules in Splunk Enterprise Security

solutions.value: Upgrade Splunk Enterprise Security and Splunk App for PCI Compliance to version 8.7.0 or higher.

descriptions.value:
In Splunk Enterprise Security versions below 8.7.0, a user that holds a role with the ueba_finding_exclusion_edit capability could create a finding exclusion rule that references an attacker-controlled lookup definition if the role also grants write access to globally shared lookup definitions, as the "ess_analyst" Splunk Enterprise Security role does. The User and Entity Behavior Analytics (UEBA) Content App could later include the lookup name in a search and run arbitrary Search Processing Language (SPL) commands with elevated permissions. With this access, the user who created the finding exclusion rule could expose stored credentials and other data outside the permissions assigned to the "ess_analyst" role.
The vulnerability is possible because UEBA finding exclusion processing does not safely quote lookup names before including them in SPL searches.
For more information see Finding exclusions in Splunk Enterprise Security (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/administer/8.3/user-and-entity-behavior-analytics/finding-exclusions-in-splunk-enterprise-security) and Roles and knowledge objects in UEBA for Splunk Enterprise Security (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/administer/8.8/user-and-entity-behavior-analytics/ueba-content-app-for-on-premises/roles-and-knowledge-objects-in-ueba-for-splunk-enterprise-security) in the Splunk documentation.

descriptions.value:
In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.6.1, 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, a low-privileged user who does not hold the "admin" or "power" Splunk roles could inject a malicious script into the name of a private saved search. If another user subsequently enables, disables, or edits the corresponding platform alert in the Monitoring Console, the injected script executes within that user's browser session, potentially allowing the low-privileged user to view sensitive information or modify data in Splunk Enterprise.
The vulnerability is possible because the Monitoring Console does not safely handle saved-search names in the platform alert workflow.
For more information see Enable and configure platform alerts (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/monitor/10.4/configure-the-monitoring-console/enable-and-configure-platform-alerts) and About configuring role-based user access (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.4/manage-splunk-platform-users-and-roles/about-configuring-role-based-user-access) in the Splunk documentation.

descriptions.value:
Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via unbounded arc length in OBJECT IDENTIFIER decoding and encoding.

The content of an OBJECT IDENTIFIER or RELATIVE-OID element is passed to unpack "w*" on decode, and the arcs of an OID string to pack "w*" on encode. Perl converts each arc to or from its decimal string in time quadratic in the arc's length, and nothing limits that length.

An attacker who controls the decoded data, or an OID string passed to encode, can exhaust CPU with a single oversized arc.

solutions.value: Upgrade to Convert-ASN1 0.37 or later.

descriptions.value:
In Splunk Enterprise Security versions below 8.7.0, a user that holds a role with the run_collect capability could store attacker-controlled values in data used by the Weak Encrypted Communication report. If another user who can access the report selects an affected drilldown, Splunk Enterprise Security could run attacker-controlled Search Processing Language (SPL) commands using the permissions of the user who selects the drilldown. The user who stores the values could then access sensitive data and modify some data available to the user who selects the drilldown.
The vulnerability is possible because the Weak Encrypted Communication report does not validate source, destination, and Secure Sockets Layer version values before inserting them into drilldown searches.
For more information see Define roles on the Splunk platform with capabilities (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.4/manage-splunk-platform-users-and-roles/define-roles-on-the-splunk-platform-with-capabilities) and Weak Encrypted Communication (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/splunk-app-for-pci-compliance/installation-and-configuration-manual/8.7/configure-reports/weak-encrypted-communication) in the Splunk documentation.

references.name: Unescaped VersionId in delete_multiple_objects: XML injection

descriptions.value:
XML Injection vulnerability in ex-aws ex_aws_s3 allows an attacker who controls an object version id passed to ExAws.S3.delete_multiple_objects/3 to add objects to the batch delete.

delete_multiple_objects/3 in lib/ex_aws/s3.ex builds the <Delete> request body by placing each object's version between <VersionId> tags without XML escaping. A version such as v1</VersionId></Object><Object><Key>important-file</Key></Object><Object><Key>x</Key><VersionId>v2 closes the caller's object and opens new ones, so S3 deletes objects the application never listed, including other users' objects in the same bucket.

This issue affects ex_aws_s3: from 2.0.0 before 2.6.0.

2. The attacker sends the key `my-own-file` and the version `v1</VersionId></Object><Object><Key>important-file</Key></Object><Object><Key>x</Key><VersionId>v2`.
3. `delete_multiple_objects/3` interpolates the version unescaped into the `<Delete>` body.

x_technicalAnalysis.value:
1. Selective escaping. When delete_multiple_objects/3 in lib/ex_aws/s3.ex builds the <Delete> body, it escapes each object's key with escape_xml_string/1 but emits the version from the same tuple raw: "<VersionId>", version, "</VersionId>".

2. Element break-out. XML metacharacters in version are read as markup. A value beginning </VersionId></Object> closes the current object early, and the rest of the string can open further <Object>...</Object> elements while keeping the document well-formed.

3. Extra deletes. The body POSTed to S3 lists more delete targets than the caller passed in, so a single crafted version id removes arbitrary additional objects in the bucket.

descriptions.value:
In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, a user who holds the "power" Splunk role could create and share a dashboard that contains attacker-controlled Search Processing Language (SPL). The SPL could run using the permissions of the user who opens the dashboard. With this access, the user who created the dashboard could expose stored credentials and write data to an index.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk Enterprise does not correctly escape field names in searches that use the rename command.
For more information see rename (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/spl-search-reference/10.4/search-commands/rename) and SPL safeguards for risky commands (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.4/best-practices-for-splunk-platform-security/spl-safeguards-for-risky-commands) in the Splunk documentation.

Splunk SOAR then flags the task as overdue immediately and does not display the configured deadline in the work queue. The incorrect deadline status could obscure genuine deadline breaches.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk SOAR treats an absent phase-level or task-level service-level agreement as immediately due when it compares the configured due times.
For more information see Define tasks using workbooks (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/administer-soar-on-premises/7.0.0/configure-product-settings-for-your-splunk-soar-on-premises-instance/define-tasks-using-workbooks) in the Splunk documentation.

descriptions.value:
United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A OCPP UpdateFirmware Out-Of-Bounds Write Remote Code Execution Vulnerability. This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A EV chargers. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in a write past the end of an allocated buffer. An attacker can leverage this in conjunction with other vulnerabilities to execute code in the context of the device. Was ZDI-CAN-29487.

cna.title: Insufficient validation of payment status for Stripe

descriptions.value:
Our payment integration with Stripe did not properly validate payment status responses. An attacker could use a successful payment status response from one payment and supply it to the system for a different payment, gaining access to multiple valid tickets with only one payment. However, the attack requires knowledge of a valid charge ID from the same event which we believe is usually not exposed to users.




To simplify attack surface, the fix removes support for incoming webhooks regarding payments created through Stripe's old "source" API. pretix stopped creating payments using this API in 2024.1 for most payment methods and in 2024.9 for all payment methods.

solutions.value: Upgrade Splunk Enterprise Security and Splunk App for PCI Compliance to version 8.7.0 or higher.

workarounds.value:
The vulnerability affects instances with Splunk Web turned on. Turning Splunk Web off is a possible workaround.
See [Disable unnecessary Splunk Enterprise components](https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.6/install-splunk-enterprise-securely/disable-unnecessary-splunk-enterprise-components) and the [web.conf](https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/admin-manual/10.6/configuration-file-reference/10.6.0-configuration-file-reference/web.conf) configuration specification file for more information on turning off Splunk Web.

descriptions.value:
In Splunk Enterprise Security versions below 8.7.0, a user that holds a role with the run_collect capability could store attacker-controlled certificate values. If another user who can access the Secure Sockets Layer Search dashboard selects an affected row, Splunk Enterprise Security could run attacker-controlled Search Processing Language (SPL) commands using the permissions of the user who selects the row. The user who stores the values could then access sensitive data and modify data available to the user who selects the row.
The vulnerability is possible because the Secure Sockets Layer Search dashboard encodes certificate values for the drilldown link but does not escape the values as SPL search literals before inserting the values into drilldown searches.
For more information see Define roles on the Splunk platform with capabilities (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.4/manage-splunk-platform-users-and-roles/define-roles-on-the-splunk-platform-with-capabilities) and Protocol intelligence dashboards (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/user-guide/8.7/analytics/protocol-intelligence-dashboards) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, an unauthenticated user could inject arbitrary fields into Splunk Enterprise audit records via the Representational State Transfer (REST) API. 
Successful exploitation could allow the unauthenticated user to forge audit evidence, compromising the integrity of audit reviews and security detections that rely on legacy audit-field parsing.
The vulnerability exists because Splunk Enterprise does not neutralize field delimiters in user-supplied data before writing the data to a legacy audit record. The affected workflow also does not create a corresponding structured audit record.

Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via a declared element length passed unchecked to sysread in asn_read and asn_get.

The length an element declares in its BER header is passed to sysread as the read size. Perl grows the target buffer to that size before reading, so memory is allocated from the declared length, not from the data received. A 6-byte header can declare a length of up to 4GB.

A single header makes the reading process allocate the declared size. Where the allocation fails, perl exits with "Out of memory", which eval cannot catch.

solutions.value: Upgrade to Convert-ASN1 0.37 or later.

cna.title: Unsafe usage of return values

descriptions.value: pretix offloads certain processes to background tasks that are run by a different server to avoid HTTP workers being clogged with processes that take longer than a usual web request. The browser periodically polls the server to see if the task is already finished using a UUID-shaped task ID. Once the task is completed, pretix resumes to the next step of the operation based on the result of the task. The system does however not check if the result stems from the correct type of task. Therefore, an attacker can supply the UUID of a task of a different type and pretix will continue with the result from the wrong task. In most cases, this will just result in an error because the return types do not match up, but in some cases this can be abused to extract objects the attacker usually should not see. Specifically, a vector was discovered that allowed to abuse this for unauthorized access to other people's ticket purchases. The attacker can, however, not control which purchases they get access to.

allow an authenticated contact user to access information associated with other

is limited to information disclosure and does not extend existing modification
or command execution permissions. This issue is resolved in ConnectWise
Automate 2026.11.

In Splunk Enterprise Security versions below 8.7.0, a user that holds a role with the run_collect capability could store attacker-controlled values in managed-lookup audit data. If another user who can access the Managed Lookups Audit dashboard selects an affected row, Splunk Enterprise Security could run attacker-controlled Search Processing Language (SPL) commands using the permissions of the user who selects the row. The user who stores the values could then access sensitive data and modify some data available to the user who selects the row.
The vulnerability is possible because the Managed Lookups Audit dashboard does not safely escape audit data before inserting it into drilldown searches.
For more information see Define roles on the Splunk platform with capabilities (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.4/manage-splunk-platform-users-and-roles/define-roles-on-the-splunk-platform-with-capabilities) and Audit dashboards (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/user-guide/8.7/analytics/audit-dashboards) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, an operator of a configured identity provider could authenticate as an existing user associated with another configured identity provider. If that account has the "Administrator" Splunk SOAR role, the operator could control the Splunk SOAR deployment.
Splunk SOAR does not bind external user accounts to the identity provider that provisions them and authenticates accounts by username without verifying provider ownership.

For more information see Configure single sign-on authentication (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/administer-soar-on-premises/8.7.0/manage-your-splunk-soar-on-premises-users-and-accounts/configure-single-sign-on-authentication-for-splunk-soar-on-premises) and Manage roles and permissions (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/administer-soar-on-premises/8.8.0/manage-your-splunk-soar-on-premises-users-and-accounts/manage-roles-and-permissions-in-splunk-soar-on-premises) in the Splunk documentation.

source.value: Hyeongseok Lee (@fluorite_pwn), Yunje Shin (@YunjeShin), Chaeeul Hyun (@yskm_Gunter), Ingyu Yang (@Mafty5275), Hoseok Kang (@clay419), Seungyeon Park (@vvsy46), and Wonjun Choi (@won6_choi) of BoB::Takedown

descriptions.value:
United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A FTP URL Path Parsing Stack-based Buffer Overflow Remote Code Execution Vulnerability. This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A EV chargers. descriptions.value: The UiChemy – Convert Figma, Prompts and AI Builds to Elementor, Gutenberg and Bricks plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the 'head' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 5.6.1 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with editor-level access and above, to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. On a default single-site WordPress installation, Editors hold the 'unfiltered_html' capability, meaning the plugin's only effective gate passes for Editor-level users, and the secondary UiChemy_Roles check is a no-op on the Free build and default Pro configuration.

descriptions.value: The WPZOOM Forms – Drag & Drop Contact Form Builder for WordPress plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to authorization bypass in all versions up to, and including, 2.0.12 This is due to the plugin not properly verifying that a user is authorized to perform an action. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with contributor-level access and above, to view the Name, Email address, and message excerpt stored in the _wpzf_fields meta of every form submission site-wide, regardless of submission ownership. solutions.value: Upgrade Splunk Enterprise versions 10.6.1, 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17 or higher.

descriptions.value:
In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, a low-privileged user who holds the "power" Splunk role could inject arbitrary Search Processing Language (SPL) commands into a Classic Dashboard search. When another user opens the affected dashboard in Splunk Web, those injected commands execute with the viewing user's permissions, potentially allowing the low-privileged user to access stored credentials and write data to indexes.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk Enterprise does not correctly escape user-supplied content when it rewrites a search, which lets the rewritten search include additional SPL commands.
The vulnerability requires another user to open the dashboard in Splunk Web. Consequently, a user who holds the "power" Splunk role should not be able to exploit the vulnerability at will.
For more information see SPL safeguards for risky commands (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.6/best-practices-for-splunk-platform-security/spl-safeguards-for-risky-commands) and Define roles on the Splunk platform with capabilities (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.6/manage-splunk-platform-users-and-roles/define-roles-on-the-splunk-platform-with-capabilities) in the Splunk documentation.

The vulnerability is possible because the REST API for approvals exposes the live external prompt link without verifying that the requester owns the approval.

descriptions.value: NocoDB before 2026.10.1 contains a stored HTML injection vulnerability that allows authenticated users with record edit rights to inject forms, images, and styled overlays into rich text cells, which are sanitized only with DOMPurify's default policy. Attackers can place a page-sized spoofed sign-in form or remote image in a cell to harvest passwords and disclose viewer IP addresses in expanded records, gallery and kanban cards, and shared views.

cna.title: Bazarr: Authenticated path traversal (arbitrary file read & write) in subtitle operations due to missing path containment

descriptions.value: Bazarr is a companion application to Sonarr and Radarr. Prior to 1.6.3-beta.11, the /api/subtitles/subtitles-info handler uses SubtitleNameContents.get() in subtitles_contents.py and reads the caller-supplied subtitlePath after checking only its subtitle extension; because the resolved path is not confined to files indexed by Bazarr, traversal can read files outside the media library. The /api/subtitles/subtitles handler in subtitles.py passes caller-supplied path and reference to sync and translation without per-path authorization, allowing an out-of-library reference file to be read and output to overwrite a file outside the media library. The authenticate decorator gates both endpoints when API authentication is enabled, while auth = None allows access without credentials. Both paths can affect only files that the Bazarr process can read or write. This issue is fixed in version 1.6.3-beta.11.

descriptions.description: CWE-22: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory

descriptions.value: react-native-webview 13.8.0 through 17.1.0 contains a code injection vulnerability that allows attackers to execute JavaScript by placing unescaped backticks or ${} sequences in injectedJavaScriptObject string values. Attackers who control values like profile fields or API responses can break out of the template literal to access the page DOM, non-HttpOnly cookies, and the ReactNativeWebView message bridge.

descriptions.description: Improper Control of Generation of Code ('Code Injection')

cna.title: NocoDB before 2026.10.1 OAuth Access Token Accepted as First-Party Session

descriptions.value: NocoDB before 2026.10.1 contains an authentication bypass vulnerability that allows OAuth token holders to act as full sessions because OAuth access tokens are signed with the instance JWT secret. Attackers can present a narrowly scoped OAuth token to the session strategy, short-lived-token exchange, or NocoSocket handshake to gain the granting user's full privileges.

descriptions.value: Traefik from 2.11.58 before 2.11.61 contains a resource leak vulnerability that allows unauthenticated attackers to exhaust resources by sending Authorization headers with NTLM or Negotiate schemes. Attackers can open many short-lived connections that each allocate a dedicated backend transport never released, exhausting memory, file descriptors and backend connections.
