descriptions.value:
MISP's LDAP authentication components (LdapAuth plugin and Apache LDAP authentication) unconditionally re-enabled user accounts that had been disabled by an administrator. During the user provisioning or update step of an LDAP login, the disabled flag was reset to enabled regardless of the account's current state.

This allowed any user with valid LDAP credentials to bypass an administrative disable action simply by authenticating, effectively nullifying the ability to revoke access through account deactivation.

- Affects the LdapAuth plugin and the ApacheSecureAuth component
- The insecure behavior was the default; no special configuration was required to trigger it
- An administrator's decision to disable a user (e.g., after a security incident or employee departure) could be reversed by the user's next successful LDAP login

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52
CAPEC-12 Application Configuration Error

solutions.value: The fix introduces an 'unblock' configuration option (default: false) to both the LdapAuth plugin and ApacheSecureAuth component. When unblock is false (the new default), a disabled user is refused authentication after the user record update, and the disabled flag is preserved. When explicitly set to true, the previous re-enable-on-login behavior is restored. A new test suite validates that disabled users are refused by default and that the unblock option correctly restores the legacy behavior.

cna.title: MISP LDAP Authentication Bypasses Disabled User Status on Login

assumptions: The affected version range is inferred from the explicit context (affected_version: 0, fixed_version: 2.5.52); the patch itself does not enumerate all affected versions.
CVSS PR:L assumes the attacker already possesses valid LDAP credentials for a disabled MISP account; if credential theft is a prerequisite, the effective attack complexity may be higher.
CAPEC-12 is the closest available mapping; the vulnerability is more precisely an insecure default in authentication logic rather than a pure configuration error.
The CVSS impact metrics (VI:L) reflect the direct modification of the disabled flag; the downstream impact of a re-enabled user accessing data is not separately scored.
The commit date (2026-11-16) and fixed version (2.5.52) are taken from the supplied metadata; no independent verification of version boundaries was performed.

capecRationale.rationale: The insecure behavior (unconditional re-enable of disabled users on LDAP login) was the default configuration. No attacker action beyond a normal login was needed; the default code path was the vulnerable path. CAPEC-12 is the closest available match because the vulnerability stemmed from an insecure default behavior in the application's authentication logic. Uncertainty: this is more precisely a code logic flaw than a pure configuration error, but no CAPEC entry specifically covers 'insecure default authentication behavior that bypasses authorization state.'

AC:L: exploitation requires only a standard LDAP login with valid credentials; no race conditions or special timing. AT:N: no manipulation of the attack target is needed. PR:L: valid LDAP credentials for a disabled MISP account are required. UI:N: no user interaction beyond the attacker's own login. VC:N: the vulnerability does not directly expose new confidential data; the attacker already possesses valid credentials. VI:L: the integrity impact is limited to the disabled flag being modified (authorization state compromised). VA:N: no availability impact on the MISP service itself. SC/SI/SA:N: no secondary system impact is evidenced.

When unblock is false (the new default), a disabled user is refused authentication after the user record update, and the disabled flag is preserved. When explicitly set to true, the previous re-enable-on-login behavior is restored. A new test suite validates that disabled users are refused by default and that the unblock option correctly restores the legacy behavior.

x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: Modified LdapAuthenticate.php and ApacheAuthenticate.php to check the user's disabled status before saving and to refuse authentication (return false or throw UnauthorizedException) when the user is disabled and the unblock option is not set. Added the unblock configuration option to config.default.php and the LdapAuth README. Added a new test file LdapAuthDisabledUserTest.php with four test cases covering disabled user refusal, role/org update on refusal, re-enable with unblock=true, and normal enabled user flow.

descriptions.value:
MISP contains a DOM-based cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the Pivot Explorer component. The bundled pivotick visualization library (version 1.2.0) rendered all string values it received as HTML markup rather than as plain text. As a result, user-controllable data fields, including attribute comments, attribute values, and reference relationship types, were interpreted and executed as HTML/JavaScript in the Pivot Explorer tooltip and sidebar panels.

An authenticated user with the ability to create or modify MISP attributes could embed malicious HTML or script payloads in these fields. When another user (or the same user) opened the Pivot Explorer and viewed the affected event data, the injected markup would execute in the victim's browser context, potentially allowing session hijacking, data exfiltration, or unauthorized actions performed on behalf of the victim.

Preconditions:
- The attacker must have authenticated access to create or modify MISP attributes (comments, values, or reference relationship types).
- The victim must open the Pivot Explorer and interact with or view the affected event data in the tooltip or sidebar.

Security impact: Successful exploitation allows arbitrary script execution in the victim's browser within the MISP application origin, enabling theft of session credentials, manipulation of displayed data, and execution of privileged API calls on behalf of the victim.

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52.
CAPEC-66 XSS - DOM Based

descriptions.description: CWE-79 Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')

solutions.value: The vulnerability is remediated by upgrading the bundled pivotick library from version 1.2.0 to version 3.0.0. The updated library renders all string data as plain text rather than parsing and executing it as HTML, eliminating the injection vector in the Pivot Explorer tooltip and sidebar.

cna.title: MISP Pivot Explorer DOM-Based Cross-Site Scripting via Unsanitized Attribute Data Rendering

assumptions: The affected version range is assumed to be all MISP versions prior to 2.5.52, based on the explicit context providing affected_version '0' and fixed_version '2.5.52'. The exact starting version is not specified in the patch.

PR:L assumes the attacker needs authenticated access to create or modify MISP attributes. If MISP deployments allow unauthenticated attribute creation (unlikely but not excluded by the patch evidence), PR could be N.
UI:A assumes the victim must actively navigate to the Pivot Explorer and view the affected data. If the Pivot Explorer auto-renders on page load in some configurations, UI could be P.

The CAPEC-66 mapping is the closest match for DOM-based XSS. The exact rendering mechanism (innerHTML vs. insertAdjacentHTML vs. template injection) is not fully visible in the truncated patch, but the commit message explicitly states strings were 'parsed as HTML' and the fix renders them 'as text'.

The patch is truncated in the middle, so the full scope of code changes in pivotick.iife.js could not be fully verified. The analysis relies on the commit message and the visible portions of the diff.

SC:H and SI:H assume the XSS can access the full MISP application session (cookies, API tokens) in the victim's browser. If the Pivot Explorer runs in a sandboxed iframe or separate origin, impact could be lower.

capecRationale.rationale: The vulnerability involves client-side rendering of untrusted data (MISP attribute comments, values, reference relationship types) as HTML in the DOM via the pivotick library's tooltip and sidebar components. The attacker injects a payload into a data field, and the victim's browser executes it when the Pivot Explorer renders the data. This matches CAPEC-66 (DOM-based XSS) precisely. No server-side reflection is involved; the injection occurs entirely in the browser's DOM.

AT:N - No attack target manipulation is needed. PR:L - The attacker requires authenticated access to create or modify MISP attributes (comments, values, reference types). UI:A - The victim must actively open the Pivot Explorer and view the affected event data for the payload to execute. VC:N, VI:N, VA:N - The vulnerable system (MISP server) is not directly impacted; the impact is on the victim's browser session. SC:H - The attacker can execute arbitrary JavaScript in the victim's browser, stealing session tokens, API keys, and displayed sensitive data. SI:H - The attacker can perform actions on behalf of the victim (create, modify, or delete events) via the compromised session. SA:N - No direct impact on security authority of the vulnerable system.

The updated library renders all string data as plain text rather than parsing and executing it as HTML, eliminating the injection vector in the Pivot Explorer tooltip and sidebar.

x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: The patch replaces the bundled pivotick.iife.js (version 1.2.0) with the pivotick 3.0.0 build, updating 536 lines of JavaScript (300 insertions, 238 deletions). The CSS file pivotick.css is also updated to match the new library's styling. The core security change is that pivotick 3.0.0 renders attribute comments, values, and reference relationship types as escaped text nodes instead of injecting them via innerHTML or equivalent DOM manipulation, preventing HTML/JS injection in the Pivot Explorer tooltip and sidebar.

cna.title: Path Rules Enforced in Front of PHP Can Be Bypassed by Appending the Path to the Script Name

descriptions.value:
Since the fix for CVE-2025-64500, Request::getPathInfo() strips the script name from the start of the URL. It does so even when the script name is only the start of a longer path segment. With SCRIPT_NAME set to /index.php, a request to /index.phpadmin gets the path info /admin and is routed like /admin. Encoded spellings such as /index%2Ephpadmin or /%69ndex.phpadmin work too. Before that fix, the path info was admin, which no route matched.

Rules enforced by Symfony are not affected: access_control and firewalls read the same path info as the router. Rules enforced in front of PHP are. The nginx configuration of the Symfony documentation and the .htaccess file of symfony/apache-pack make /index.php/admin unreachable, but they pass /index.phpadmin to the front controller. So a location /admin block in nginx, a <Location /admin> section in Apache, or a CDN or WAF rule on /admin can be bypassed.

The script name is now stripped only when it is followed by /, ? or the end of the URL. A request to /index.phpadmin gets the path info /index.phpadmin.

supportingMedia.value:
Since the fix for CVE-2025-64500, `Request::getPathInfo()` strips the script name from the start of the URL. It does so even when the script name is only the start of a longer path segment. With `SCRIPT_NAME` set to `/index.php`, a request to `/index.phpadmin` gets the path info `/admin` and is routed like `/admin`. Encoded spellings such as `/index%2Ephpadmin` or `/%69ndex.phpadmin` work too. Before that fix, the path info was `admin`, which no route matched.

Rules enforced by Symfony are not affected: `access_control` and firewalls read the same path info as the router. Rules enforced in front of PHP are. The nginx configuration of the Symfony documentation and the `.htaccess` file of `symfony/apache-pack` make `/index.php/admin` unreachable, but they pass `/index.phpadmin` to the front controller. So a `location /admin` block in nginx, a `<Location /admin>` section in Apache, or a CDN or WAF rule on `/admin` can be bypassed.

The script name is now stripped only when it is followed by `/`, `?` or the end of the URL. A request to `/index.phpadmin` gets the path info `/index.phpadmin`.

cna.title: open62541 1.5.0-1.5.10 Use-After-Free via RelativePath Parsing

descriptions.value: open62541 1.5.0 through 1.5.10 contains a use-after-free and double free vulnerability in the lookupRefType() function in src/util/ua_util.c that allows attackers to corrupt the heap of the server process by supplying a RelativePath string resolved through UA_RelativePath_parseWithServer(). When the path names a ReferenceType with a string or GUID NodeId, the function returns a shallow copy of the browse result's NodeId and frees its identifier, causing the identifier to be freed a second time when the parsed path is cleared, which attackers can exploit to crash the server process.

references.name: VulnCheck Advisory: open62541 1.5.0-1.5.10 Use-After-Free via RelativePath Parsing

cna.title: Incorrect authorization in whereDoesntHave morph-map handling in Laravel MongoDB

descriptions.value: A polymorphic relationship query helper in the MongoDB Eloquent integration for Laravel resolves a record's type identifier inconsistently between the code that stores a relationship link and the code that searches for one. An application that relies on a relationship-absence query to restrict which records a request may see or change can therefore have that restriction silently fail, allowing a user with basic application privileges to read and to modify or remove records the restriction was meant to cover.

descriptions.value:
MISP contains a type confusion vulnerability in the authentication key creation endpoint. When a user submits a floating-point value as the target user identifier, the authorization check truncates the value to an integer (matching the attacker's own account), while the persistence layer rounds the same value to a different integer (the next account in the sequence). This discrepancy allows an authenticated user with key-creation permission to generate an API authentication key belonging to another user.

Preconditions:
- The attacker must be an authenticated user with the permission to create authentication keys.
- The target user must have a consecutive numeric identifier immediately following the attacker's identifier.

Impact:
- Unauthorized creation of an API key for another user, granting the attacker access to that user's data and operations within the MISP instance.
- The vulnerability is trivially exploitable by substituting a carefully crafted floating-point value for the integer user identifier in the request.

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52.
CAPEC-15 Using Excessive Floating Point Precision
CAPEC-110 Parameter Tampering

solutions.value: The fix enforces strict type validation on the user identifier parameter in both the controller and the model layer. Only native integers or digit-only strings are accepted; any other type (including floating-point numbers) is rejected with an authorization error before the value reaches the persistence layer. This eliminates the discrepancy between the authorization check and the storage layer, preventing the type confusion from being exploited.

cna.title: MISP Auth Key Creation Type Confusion Allows Unauthorized Key for Adjacent User

ai_annotations.description: Draft vulnerability metadata was generated from a git-format patch using an Ollama-hosted language model. Human validation is required before publication.

assumptions: The affected version range is inferred from the explicit context (fixed in 2.5.52); the patch itself does not enumerate all prior affected versions.
PR:L assumes the attacker needs only the standard perm_auth role; the patch does not specify whether additional roles or configurations are required.

CAPEC-15 is the closest available mapping; the vulnerability is more precisely a type-confusion between integer and float handling rather than a pure precision-excess issue, but no CAPEC entry specifically covers integer/float type confusion in authorization checks.

The CVSS impact metrics (VC:L, VI:L) assume the attacker gains meaningful access to the adjacent user's data; the actual scope of data accessible depends on the target user's role and permissions, which are not specified in the patch.
The Co-Authored-By line references Claude Opus 5.5 as an AI assistant; it is not credited as a person or organization.

capecRationale.rationale: The vulnerability is directly caused by a floating-point value being accepted where an integer is expected. The float passes an integer-truncation check but is stored with floating-point rounding that produces a different integer. This is a textbook case of floating-point precision/type handling causing an unintended security outcome. The mapping is a close fit because the core mechanism is the discrepancy in how a float is interpreted by two different code paths.

The attacker tampers with the user_id parameter by supplying a crafted floating-point value instead of the expected integer, exploiting the type-handling inconsistency. This is a secondary mapping; the primary mechanism is the floating-point precision issue (CAPEC-15), but the attack vector is parameter manipulation.

x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In AuthKeysController::add(), a guard clause is added before the existing authorization logic that rejects any user_id that is neither a native PHP integer nor a string consisting solely of digits (ctype_digit), throwing a MethodNotAllowedException. The value is then explicitly cast to int. In AuthKey::canCreateAuthKeyForUser(), an identical type check is added for non-site-admin users, returning false if the user_id is not an integer or digit string. A regression test class (AuthKeyAddCanonicalUserId) is added to tests/testregressions.py that verifies: (1) a float user_id that truncates to the attacker's ID but rounds to the next user's ID is rejected with HTTP 400+, (2) legitimate integer and digit-string forms still work, and (3) a plain integer for another user is still refused by the existing authorization logic.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The root cause is that the user_id parameter accepts a floating-point value where only an integer should be permitted. The authorization check and the persistence layer interpret the float differently, but the fundamental weakness is the failure to validate and reject non-integer input types at the boundary.

The practical security impact is a bypass of the authorization check: the (int) cast in the permission check matches the attacker's own ID, while the ORM saves a different ID, effectively granting access to another user's resources without proper authorization.

descriptions.value:
MISP contains a vulnerability in its password reset (forgot password) functionality where the base URL used to construct the reset link sent by email could be derived from the HTTP request's Host header rather than from an explicitly configured value.

An unauthenticated attacker can send a crafted request with a malicious Host header. If the application's base URL was not explicitly configured (MISP.baseurl or MISP.external_baseurl), the bootstrap would derive it from the request, and the resulting password reset email would contain a link pointing to the attacker-controlled domain. When the victim clicks the link, they are directed to the attacker's site, enabling credential phishing or token theft.

Preconditions:
- The password reset feature (allow_password_forgotten) is enabled
- MISP.baseurl and MISP.external_baseurl are not explicitly set to trusted values
- The victim initiates or is targeted for a password reset

Impact:
- Phishing: victim is redirected to an attacker-controlled URL instead of the legitimate MISP instance
- Potential credential compromise if the victim enters credentials on the attacker's site
- No direct compromise of the MISP server itself

Affected: MISP versions prior to 2.5.52
CAPEC-60 Leverage Executable Content

solutions.value: The fix ensures that password reset links are constructed exclusively from explicitly configured base URLs (MISP.baseurl or MISP.external_baseurl). A new internal flag (BaseurlFromRequest) marks base URLs derived from the HTTP request as untrusted for outbound mail. If no trusted base URL is available, the reset email is not sent and an error is logged. An empty external_baseurl now correctly falls back to the configured baseurl rather than the request-derived value.

cna.title: MISP Password Reset Link Host Header Injection Enables Phishing via Untrusted Base URL

The affected version range is assumed to be all versions prior to 2.5.52; the explicit context lists affected_version as '0' which is treated as a placeholder for 'all prior versions'.
CAPEC-60 is selected as the closest plausible attack pattern; no CAPEC specifically addresses Host header injection for outbound link construction, so this mapping carries uncertainty.

The CVSS SC:L rating assumes the primary impact is potential credential phishing of the end user; if the attacker could also forge the reset token flow to directly set a password, the impact could be higher, but the patch evidence does not confirm that scenario.

AT:N is assumed because the attacker does not need to set up special infrastructure beyond having a domain to receive the redirected traffic; this is a minimal requirement inherent to any phishing attack.

capecRationale.rationale: The attacker leverages the application's processing of the Host header (executable content in the sense that it is interpreted and used to generate an outbound URL) to redirect the password reset link to an attacker-controlled domain. This is the closest CAPEC to a Host header injection / open redirect in an outbound email context. Uncertainty: no CAPEC specifically covers Host header manipulation for outbound link construction; CAPEC-60 is selected as the best available match describing an attacker exploiting application-processed input to achieve an unintended output.

x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N: The attack is performed over the network via a crafted HTTP request. AC:L: The attacker only needs to send a request with a modified Host header; no race conditions or complex timing required. AT:N: No need to bypass or prepare against specific mitigations. PR:N: The forgot-password endpoint is accessible without authentication. UI:A: The victim must actively click the malicious link in the received email for the attack to succeed. VC/VI/VA:N: The MISP server itself is not directly compromised; no data is exfiltrated from or modified on the server. SC:L: The subsequent impact is on the user, whose credentials may be phished via the attacker-controlled URL. SI/SA:N: No integrity or availability impact on the user or their systems beyond the potential credential theft captured in SC.

A new internal flag (BaseurlFromRequest) marks base URLs derived from the HTTP request as untrusted for outbound mail. If no trusted base URL is available, the reset email is not sent and an error is logged. An empty external_baseurl now correctly falls back to the configured baseurl rather than the request-derived value.

x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In bootstrap.default.php, a new Configure key 'BaseurlFromRequest' is set to true when the base URL is derived from SERVER_NAME/SERVER_PORT. In User.php (forgot method), the base URL resolution logic is replaced: it first checks MISP.external_baseurl, then checks if BaseurlFromRequest is true (in which case it refuses to send the email and logs an error), otherwise falls back to MISP.baseurl. If no valid base URL is found, the function returns false without sending mail. Server.php updates the setting description to document the new requirement. A new test file (PasswordResetBaseurlTest.php) with six test cases validates all base URL resolution scenarios including request-derived rejection, configured URL usage, external URL preference, and empty-external fallback.

In Eclipse Ditto versions 1.1.0 to 3.9.9, the nginx reverse proxy configurations shipped with Ditto (Helm chart, Docker Compose, Kubernetes and OpenShift deployment files) forward a client-supplied

  `x-ditto-pre-authenticated` header to the Ditto gateway on locations that do not apply nginx authentication, such as `/api/2/connections`. nginx selects the location based on the normalized request URI
  but forwards the raw URI, while the gateway does not treat an encoded slash (`%2f`) as a path separator. A crafted request path is therefore routed by nginx through such an unauthenticated location and
  by the gateway to the regular Things and Policies HTTP API, including routes that send live messages to devices. When pre-authentication is enabled (the default of the Helm chart and the Docker Compose
  setup), an unauthenticated remote attacker can impersonate arbitrary policy subjects and read, modify and delete Things, read Policies, send messages to devices and create entities. Additionally, the
  optional Ingress of the Helm chart (Ditto 3.9.0 to 3.9.9) routes requests directly to the gateway without setting or removing that header, and the WebSocket Ingress of the Helm chart of Ditto 3.3.0 to
  3.8.15 does not set it, allowing the same impersonation without path manipulation when pre-authentication is enabled. This bypasses the fix for CVE-2026-120753.

descriptions.value:
MISP is vulnerable to Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) in its correlation management functionality.

The top-correlation cache regeneration and occurrence count regeneration actions were accessible via bodyless GET requests and were triggered from the admin interface using plain hyperlinks rather than POST forms. Because these state-changing operations did not require a POST method and were reachable through simple URL navigation, an attacker who can induce an authenticated administrator to visit a malicious page or click a crafted link can trigger these operations without the administrator's explicit consent.

Impact:
- Unintended triggering of resource-intensive correlation regeneration processes
- Potential disruption of correlation data processing and increased server load
- No direct data disclosure or corruption is evidenced

Affected: MISP versions prior to 2.5.52
CAPEC-123 Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)

solutions.value: The vulnerability is remediated by enforcing the HTTP POST method on both the top-correlation cache regeneration and occurrence count regeneration controller actions, rejecting any GET request with a 405 Method Not Allowed response. The admin interface views are updated to render these actions as POST forms instead of plain hyperlinks, ensuring that the state-changing operations cannot be triggered by a simple URL reference in a third-party page.

The CAPEC-123 mapping is considered high-confidence because the commit message and code changes explicitly describe the GET-to-POST enforcement as the security remediation for a reported issue.

descriptions.value:
MISP contains a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in its feed and sync HTTP request handling. When the application uses libcurl as the HTTP transport, the CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION option was enabled by default, causing the library to automatically follow HTTP redirects without the application's own per-hop validation logic being invoked.

- Feed requests: MISP implements its own redirect validation for feed sources, but libcurl was following redirects before that validation could execute, allowing a malicious or compromised feed source to redirect the request to arbitrary internal URLs.
- Sync requests: Sync peers are server-configured, and the application does not perform per-hop redirect validation for sync traffic. libcurl's automatic redirect following allowed a malicious sync peer to redirect the request to internal network resources.

An attacker who is a configured sync peer, controls a feed source URL, or can influence DNS resolution for a configured endpoint can exploit this to cause the MISP server to issue requests to arbitrary internal services, potentially reading sensitive data or interacting with internal APIs that are not otherwise exposed.

Affected: MISP versions prior to 2.5.52.
CAPEC-12 Exploiting Trusted Domain's URL Parsing Errors

descriptions.description: CWE-601 URL Redirection to Untrusted Site ('Open Redirect')

solutions.value: The fix disables libcurl's automatic redirect following (CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION) for both feed and sync HTTP sockets. A new private helper method checks whether the socket is a CurlClient instance and explicitly sets follow-redirects to false. This ensures that feed redirects are handled by MISP's own per-hop validation logic, and sync requests remain pinned to the configured URL, preventing the server from being directed to arbitrary internal targets via redirect responses.

cna.title: Docker Engine race in docker cp lets a container write through read-only bind mounts

descriptions.value: A malicious container can make a read-only bind mount writable while a docker cp into it is running, and the archive being copied can then create or overwrite files in the host directory behind the mount. The attacker does not choose the content written, which comes from the archive supplied by whoever runs the copy, and cannot start the copy, which requires an operator or API client. The mount is temporary, but files written through it persist after the copy completes.

workarounds.value: Do not copy files into running containers that run untrusted workloads. Stop the container before copying files into it. Use authorization plugins to restrict access to PUT /containers/{id}/archive.

descriptions.value: A race condition during docker cp mount setup in Docker Engine allows a malicious container to leave a read-only bind mount writable while an archive is extracted into the container. When copying files into a container, the daemon bind-mounts the container's volumes into a temporary view and applies the read-only flags afterwards, through a path inside the container's filesystem. A process in the container can change that path in between, so the flags are applied to a different mount and the intended bind mount stays writable for the duration of the copy.

configurations.value: The container has at least one read-only bind mount, a process inside the running container can modify a path leading to that mount's destination, and an operator or API client copies files into the container with docker cp or PUT /containers/{id}/archive. Containers without read-only bind mounts, stopped containers, and copies out of a container (GET and HEAD on /containers/{id}/archive) are not affected. Rootless Docker Engine is affected, but the impact is limited to files accessible to the daemon's user.

MISP trusted client-supplied forwarded IP headers (such as X-Forwarded-For) without verifying that the request originated from a known proxy or that the value was a valid IP address. The configured header value was accepted as the authoritative client IP for all security-relevant functions.

An unauthenticated remote attacker could forge the forwarded header to:
- Bypass IP-based restrictions on API authentication keys
- Evade brute-force / rate-limiting protection
- Inject arbitrary values into application and ECS logs, corrupting audit trails

The vulnerability required the MISP.log_client_ip_header setting to be configured to a forwarded header (e.g. HTTP_X_FORWARDED_FOR), which is a common deployment when MISP sits behind a reverse proxy.

Affected: MISP versions prior to 2.5.52
CAPEC-126 Spoofing HTTP Headers

descriptions.description: CWE-345 Insufficient Verification of Data Authenticity

solutions.value: The fix introduces a dedicated client-IP resolution routine that only honours the forwarded header when the request's peer address matches a newly introduced trusted-proxy list (MISP.trusted_proxies, supporting IPs and CIDR ranges). It selects the right-most address in the chain that does not belong to a trusted proxy, validates the result as a well-formed IP, and falls back to the TCP peer address (REMOTE_ADDR) when the header is absent, the request did not come from a listed proxy, or the value is not a valid IP. This prevents untrusted clients from injecting arbitrary values into IP-based security controls and logs.

cna.title: MISP: Client IP Spoofing via Unvalidated Forwarded Header Bypasses IP Restrictions and Brute-Force Protection

ai_annotations.description: Draft vulnerability metadata was generated from a git-format patch using an Ollama-hosted language model. Human validation is required before publication.

assumptions: The affected version range is assumed to be all MISP versions prior to 2.5.52 based on the explicit context fixed_version; the patch does not enumerate specific prior versions.

PR:N is assigned because at least one impact path (brute-force protection bypass, log forgery) is reachable without authentication; the auth-key IP restriction bypass path does require a valid API key.
CAPEC-126 is the closest available match; no CAPEC specifically covers 'unvalidated forwarded-IP header' so the general HTTP header spoofing pattern is used.
The vulnerability requires MISP.log_client_ip_header to be set to a forwarded header (not the default REMOTE_ADDR); deployments using the default are not affected.
VA:L reflects the potential for rate-limiting bypass to enable resource exhaustion; direct DoS is not demonstrated in the patch.

capecRationale.rationale: The attacker forges the X-Forwarded-For (or equivalent) HTTP header to present a spoofed client IP to the application, bypassing IP-based access restrictions and rate-limiting. This is the most direct CAPEC match: the vulnerability is specifically the lack of validation on a client-supplied HTTP header that the application treats as authoritative. No other CAPEC more precisely describes header-spoofing to defeat IP-based controls.

x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N – exploitable over the network via a crafted HTTP header. AC:L – sending a spoofed X-Forwarded-For header is trivial and requires no special conditions. AT:N – no attack-target manipulation needed. PR:N – brute-force protection bypass and log forgery require no authentication; auth-key IP restriction bypass requires a valid key but the unauthenticated paths are sufficient. UI:N – no user interaction. VC:N – no confidentiality impact on the MISP instance itself. VI:L – integrity impact from log forgery and defeat of IP-based access controls. VA:L – availability impact from brute-force / rate-limiting bypass enabling credential-stuffing or resource exhaustion. SC/SI/SA:N – no demonstrated impact on other systems.
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The fix introduces a dedicated client-IP resolution routine that only honours the forwarded header when the request's peer address matches a newly introduced trusted-proxy list (MISP.trusted_proxies, supporting IPs and CIDR ranges). It selects the right-most address in the chain that does not belong to a trusted proxy, validates the result as a well-formed IP, and falls back to the TCP peer address (REMOTE_ADDR) when the header is absent, the request did not come from a listed proxy, or the value is not a valid IP. This prevents untrusted clients from injecting arbitrary values into IP-based security controls and logs.

x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: Added a new ClientIpTool class (app/Lib/Tools/ClientIpTool.php) implementing resolve() which parses the forwarded header, cross-references entries against a trusted-proxy CIDR list, and returns the right-most non-proxy valid IP or falls back to REMOTE_ADDR. Added MISP.trusted_proxies server setting (comma-separated IPs/CIDRs) to ServerSettingGroups and Server model. Replaced the previous naive first-comma-split logic in AppModel::_remoteIp() with a call to ClientIpTool::resolve(). Updated the ECS log engine (EcsLog.php) to use the same resolution for the client.ip field. Added a comprehensive unit test suite (ClientIpToolTest.php) covering proxy chains, untrusted sources, invalid IPs, IPv6, and edge cases.

cna.title: Pion DTLS: Unbounded handshake cache allows remote memory exhaustion

descriptions.description: CWE-770: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling

descriptions.value: Pion DTLS is a Go implementation of Datagram Transport Layer Security. From 2.1.4 until 3.1.13, the handshake cache copied and retained submitted messages without deduplicating entries, limiting the entry count, limiting total payload bytes, or stopping new insertions after handshake completion. A remote peer able to deliver suitable DTLS traffic can grow the cache through incoming handshake messages and repeated caching of outgoing retransmissions for the lifetime of the connection. The fragment reassembly buffer's separate size limit does not prevent this issue because completed messages are retained in the append-only handshake cache. Unbounded cache growth can exhaust application memory and cause a denial of service. The issue is fixed in version 3.1.13.
Incorrect boundary conditions in the Graphics: Skia component. This vulnerability was fixed in Firefox 161, Firefox ESR 115.46, Firefox ESR 153.8, Thunderbird 161, and Thunderbird 153.8.

descriptions.value:
MISP contains a cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the feed and server event preview pages. When a remote MISP instance (configured as a feed source or connected server) supplies object or reference UUIDs and IDs containing special characters, these values are rendered in the preview HTML without proper escaping.

The vulnerable behavior occurs in two contexts:

- HTML element identifiers and text content: Remote UUIDs and IDs are inserted into DOM element IDs and visible text without HTML encoding, allowing injection of arbitrary HTML markup.
- Inline JavaScript event handlers: Remote UUIDs and IDs are embedded into onClick handler strings using only HTML escaping, which does not protect against JavaScript string-literal breakout. A crafted value containing a single quote can terminate the string and inject arbitrary JavaScript.

An attacker who controls a remote MISP instance (feed or server peer) can craft UUID or ID fields with a malicious payload. When an authenticated user on the victim instance views the corresponding event preview, the injected script executes in the user's browser within the MISP application origin, potentially allowing session hijacking, data exfiltration, or unauthorized actions on behalf of the user.

Affected: MISP versions prior to 2.5.52.
CAPEC-1 Cross Site Scripting

descriptions.description: CWE-79 Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')

solutions.value: The vulnerability is remediated by ensuring all remote UUID and ID values are properly escaped for their output context. In HTML contexts, values are now passed through the HTML-encoding function. In inline JavaScript handler contexts, values are serialized using JSON encoding before being HTML-encoded, producing a valid JavaScript string literal that cannot be broken out of. This prevents both HTML injection and JavaScript injection from attacker-controlled remote identifiers.

assumptions: The affected version range is inferred from the explicit context (fixed in 2.5.52); the lower bound '0' is a placeholder and the true earliest affected version is not specified in the patch.
PR:L assumes the attacker must be a configured feed or server peer; if MISP allows unauthenticated feed ingestion in some configurations, PR could be N.
UI:A assumes the victim must actively navigate to the event preview page; if the preview is auto-loaded in a workflow, UI could be P.
CAPEC-1 is the closest available mapping; the specific delivery mechanism (stored data from a remote MISP instance) does not have a more granular CAPEC entry.
The Co-Authored-By line for Claude Opus 5.5 is treated as a tool credit, not a human remediation developer.
CVSS impact metrics (VC:L, VI:L) assume the XSS can access session data and perform authenticated actions; the patch does not demonstrate a specific data-exfiltration path.

capecRationale.rationale: The attacker crafts a UUID or ID field in a remote MISP instance's data with a script payload. When the victim views the event preview, the unescaped value is rendered in the browser, executing attacker-controlled JavaScript. This is a stored XSS delivered through application data from a trusted-looking remote source. CAPEC-1 is the closest match; the specific sub-variant (stored vs. reflected) is less relevant than the core mechanism of unescaped output in a browser context.

x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N - Exploitation occurs over the network via a remote MISP feed/server connection. AC:L - The attacker only needs to set a UUID or ID field to a value containing a single quote or HTML special characters; no race conditions or special timing required. AT:N - No specific attack target configuration beyond a standard feed or server connection. PR:L - The attacker must be a configured remote MISP instance (feed or server peer), which is a low-privilege role in the MISP ecosystem. UI:A - The victim must actively navigate to the feed or server event preview page to trigger the XSS. VC:L - The injected script runs in the MISP application origin and can read session data, API tokens, or page content. VI:L - The script can perform actions on behalf of the user (submit forms, call APIs). VA:N - No direct availability impact. SC/SI/SA:N - No impact on subsequent components beyond the vulnerable web application.
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The vulnerability is remediated by ensuring all remote UUID and ID values are properly escaped for their output context. In HTML contexts, values are now passed through the HTML-encoding function. In inline JavaScript handler contexts, values are serialized using JSON encoding before being HTML-encoded, producing a valid JavaScript string literal that cannot be broken out of. This prevents both HTML injection and JavaScript injection from attacker-controlled remote identifiers.

modelComparison.selectionNotice: The selected result is closest to model consensus; this heuristic does not establish factual correctness and human review remains required.

x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: Added h() (HTML encoding) to all previously unescaped outputs of remote object UUIDs and IDs in feed and server view templates (row_attribute.ctp, row_object.ctp, row_object_reference.ctp, row_object_referenced_by.ctp for both Feeds and Servers elements). Changed inline onClick handlers in row_object_reference.ctp, row_object_referenced_by.ctp, preview_object.ctp, and object_foot.ctp to pass UUID/ID values through json_encode() before h(), converting them to safe JavaScript string literals. Added a test harness (ViewTemplateHarness.php) and a regression test (RemoteEventPreviewEscapingTest.php) that renders the affected templates with a malicious UUID payload and asserts proper escaping in both HTML and JavaScript contexts.

x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The vulnerability is remediated by eliminating the injection of untrusted GID values into inline JavaScript event handler contexts. Inline onmouseenter/onmouseleave attributes are replaced with a data-object-tooltip-gid HTML data attribute, and event handling is moved to delegated jQuery listeners in helper.js that read the value via the DOM dataset API, which does not parse the value as JavaScript. The AJAX tooltip URL now applies encodeURIComponent to the GID. Dynamically generated DOM elements are built using jQuery's .attr() and .text() methods instead of string concatenation, ensuring proper HTML and text encoding.
assumptions: The attacker is assumed to have authenticated access (PR:L) to create or modify objects with controlled GID values (filenames, message IDs). If an unauthenticated upload or creation path exists, PR could be N.
The GID values are assumed to be attacker-influenceable through filenames or message IDs as stated in the commit message; the exact input vector is not fully specified in the patch.
UI:P is assumed because the victim must hover over the affected link; if the tooltip triggers on page load or via a different mechanism, UI could be N.
No specific affected version range is identified from the patch; the version boundary is unknown.
The CAPEC-1 mapping is the closest standard pattern; a more specific sub-pattern for stored XSS via JavaScript-in-HTML-attribute injection is not separately enumerated in CAPEC.
The commit message references 'Grant and ENISA AI team' as reporters; the exact role (finder vs. reporter) is interpreted as reporter based on the word 'Reported by'.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In helper.js, two delegated event listeners (mouseenter, mouseleave) are added for elements matching a[data-object-tooltip-gid], calling show_obj_tooltip with this.dataset.objectTooltipGid. The show_obj_tooltip function now applies encodeURIComponent(obj_gid) when building the $.getJSON URL. In dashboard.html, trackers_dashboard.html, and objs_dashboard.html, all inline onmouseenter/onmouseenter attributes containing interpolated GID values are replaced with data-object-tooltip-gid attributes. In the JavaScript create_obj_svg helper functions, inline .on('mouseenter'/'mouseleave') registrations are replaced with .attr('data-object-tooltip-gid', obj_gid). descriptions.value:
The AIL Framework web application contains a stored cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in its dashboard templates. In the home dashboard (dashboard.html), the hunter trackers dashboard (trackers_dashboard.html), and the objects dashboard (objs_dashboard.html), object global identifiers (GIDs) derived from filenames or message IDs were interpolated directly into inline JavaScript event handler attributes (onmouseenter/onmouseleave) within HTML anchor tags. Because the GID value was placed inside a single-quoted JavaScript string literal within an HTML attribute, an attacker who could control the GID value (for example, by crafting a filename or message ID containing a single quote) could break out of the string context and inject arbitrary JavaScript code that would execute in the context of any user viewing the dashboard.

Additionally, in dynamically generated JavaScript code within the same templates, object identifiers were concatenated into HTML strings and inline event handler registrations without sufficient encoding, presenting a similar injection surface. The AJAX tooltip lookup also concatenated the raw GID into a URL without encoding, which could be leveraged for further manipulation.

The vulnerability requires that an attacker be able to influence the GID value stored in the application (e.g., through a file upload or message creation with a crafted name) and that a victim subsequently visits one of the affected dashboard pages and hovers over the affected object link. Successful exploitation allows execution of arbitrary JavaScript in the victim's browser session, potentially leading to session hijacking, data exfiltration, or unauthorized actions performed on behalf of the victim.

cna.title: Incomplete Fix for CVE-2026-45756: JsonPath Queries Can Still Hold a Process Through search(), match() and Chained Filters

descriptions.value:
The fix for CVE-2026-45756 lowers pcre.backtrack_limit to 10000 around each preg_match() call of the match() and search() filter functions. That limit applies to one starting position, not to one call. PCRE resets its counter at every position it tries a match from. So an unanchored pattern that stays just under the limit is paid once per byte of the subject. Each call also starts from a fresh limit, so chaining clauses in one filter multiplies the work.

Two other paths made the cost of a query grow faster than its size, without any regular expression:
- The filter evaluator scanned the whole expression for logical operators once per node. Its cost grew with the square of the number of chained clauses.
- Queries starting with $ inside a filter, like @.x == $.limit or length($.items), were evaluated again for every node the filter visits.

An application that evaluates an attacker-influenced JSONPath expression can therefore still be made to hold a PHP worker. A document of 2 MB and a query of 2.5 KB take 3.5 minutes of CPU.

JsonCrawler::find() now bounds the total regex work of one call, and throws an exception when that budget is exhausted. Filter expressions are parsed once per query, and absolute queries inside filters are evaluated once per query.

credits.value: Francois-Xavier Stellamans from the NATO Cyber Security Centre with OpenAI Daybreak support (using GPT5.6-Cyber)

descriptions.value:
MISP contains multiple flaws in its login and one-time-password (OTP) brute-force lockout mechanism that collectively weaken authentication protection.

- Lockout counter bypass: the lockout stored and matched usernames using a single-byte case-fold function. An email address containing a non-ASCII capital letter (for example a Latin-1 or Cyrillic uppercase) was never counted toward the lockout threshold, allowing unlimited failed login attempts against that account.
- Collation-folding authentication bypass: the database collation performs accent and width folding, so a Unicode variant of a valid address (e.g. a different diacritic or a full-width character) resolved to the same account during authentication while the lockout treated it as a distinct, untracked identity. An attacker could therefore authenticate as the target user using a folded alias without triggering the lockout.
- Username enumeration via NUL byte: submitting a password containing a NUL byte caused the hashing routine to raise an exception, producing an HTTP 500 response for a known account but a different response for an unknown one, disclosing valid usernames.

Preconditions: the target MISP instance is reachable over the network and the login endpoint is exposed. No prior authentication is required.

Security impact: an unauthenticated attacker can perform unlimited password-guessing against accounts whose address contains a non-ASCII capital, can authenticate as a user via a Unicode-folded alias, and can enumerate valid usernames. Successful exploitation leads to account takeover.

Affected: MISP versions prior to 2.5.52.
CAPEC-10 Password Guessing
CAPEC-65 Unicode Encoding Issue
CAPEC-15 User Enumeration

descriptions.description: CWE-307 Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts
CWE-178 Improper Handling of Case Sensitivity

solutions.value: The lockout now stores and matches usernames using a multi-byte-aware case-fold (mb_strtolower with trim), ensuring all Unicode case variants are counted under a single key. Before authentication, the submitted address is canonicalised and compared to the stored address; if they differ only by collation folding (accent or width), the authentication scope is forced to a non-matching condition so the attempt fails as an unknown account. A NUL byte in the password field is stripped before hashing, eliminating the differential 500 response that enabled username enumeration.

CVSS VI is rated Low rather than High because account takeover requires a successful password guess (brute force) or a specific Unicode alias; it is not an immediate, unconditional authentication bypass.
CVSS VC is rated Low because the NUL-byte enumeration discloses only the existence of an account, not its credentials or data.

CAPEC-65 (Unicode Encoding Issue) is the closest available pattern for the collation-folding authentication bypass; the CAPEC catalogue lacks a dedicated pattern for database-collation-based identity confusion.
The Co-Authored-By line (Claude Opus 5.5) is treated as a tool credit, not a human remediation developer, and is therefore not listed as a credit candidate.

capecRationale.rationale: The lockout bypass directly enables offline or online password guessing against accounts whose address contains a non-ASCII capital letter, and the folded-alias path allows repeated authentication attempts without the counter incrementing. This is the closest CAPEC to the primary exploitation scenario.

The root cause of both the lockout bypass and the folded-alias authentication is inconsistent Unicode handling between the application-layer case-fold and the database collation. CAPEC-65 is the best available match for attacks that exploit Unicode encoding discrepancies; the mapping is approximate because the CAPEC catalogue does not have a dedicated pattern for collation-folding authentication bypass.

The NUL-byte differential response (500 vs. non-500) allows an unauthenticated attacker to distinguish valid from invalid usernames. CAPEC-15 is the standard pattern for this class of information-disclosure attack.

x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: Added a usernameKey() helper in the Bruteforce model that returns mb_strtolower(trim($username)); replaced all prior strtolower(trim(...)) calls in insert() and isBlocklisted() with this helper. In the login controller, added a NUL-byte sanitisation step that replaces the password with an empty string if a NUL byte is present. weaknessRationale.rationale: The primary defect is that the brute-force lockout counter fails to account for certain Unicode representations of a username, effectively disabling the rate-limiting control for those accounts and permitting unlimited authentication attempts.

A NUL byte in the password field produced a 500 Internal Server Error for a known account but a different response for an unknown account, creating an observable difference that enables username enumeration.

The lockout used a single-byte case-fold that did not handle non-ASCII uppercase letters, while the database collation performed full Unicode case and accent folding, creating a mismatch between the identity used for authentication and the identity used for lockout accounting.

cna.title: Filesystem Path Treats Any Prefix Before "://" as a Root, Letting Paths Escape Their Base Directory

descriptions.value:
Most methods of Symfony\Component\Filesystem\Path rely on Path::split(), which takes everything before the first :// as the root of a path. It doesn't check that this prefix is a URI scheme, so the .. segments in that prefix are never resolved. PHP sees a scheme only at the start of a string. So /base/../x://../secret.txt is a plain local path to /secret.txt for PHP, while Path::isBasePath('/base', '/base/../x://../secret.txt') returns true. canonicalize(), join(), makeAbsolute() and makeRelative() are affected the same way.

Some applications check a path built from user input with isBasePath() or canonicalize(), and then open it. They can be made to read or write files outside the expected directory.

On Symfony 6.4 and later, the AssetMapper component builds with Path::join() the path of the files that a remote package references from its CSS. A malicious or compromised package can therefore make importmap:require or importmap:install write a file of its choice outside assets/vendor. For example, the CSS url(../../../../../public/x://shell.php) writes public/x:/shell.php.

A prefix is now a scheme only when PHP would look for a stream wrapper with that name. That is two or more letters, digits, +, - or ., followed by :// at the start of the path. Other prefixes are regular path segments, and the .. segments after them are resolved. Real schemes such as phar://, file://, vfs:// or compress.zlib:// keep working.

descriptions.value:
MISP's interactive CLI shell, when used to edit or disable a user account, did not update the user record's modification timestamp. The application's session validation mechanism relies on this timestamp to detect that a user's record has changed and to reload the user's state in all active sessions.

As a result, a user who was disabled or had their role or permissions modified through the CLI would retain their existing authenticated session and continue to operate with their previous privileges until the session naturally expired. The administrative intent to revoke or reduce access was not enforced on already-active sessions.

Preconditions:
- An administrator performs a user edit or disable action via the MISP interactive CLI shell rather than the web interface.
- The target user has one or more active web sessions at the time of the change.

Impact:
- A disabled user retains full access to the MISP instance for the duration of their existing session.
- A user whose role or permissions were reduced via the CLI continues to operate with their prior, higher privileges in open sessions.

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52.
CAPEC-66 Session Fixation

solutions.value: The CLI user edit and disable operations now include the date_modified field in the save operation's field list, ensuring the modification timestamp is updated. This causes the application's session validation logic to detect the change and reload the user's state in all open sessions, immediately reflecting the disable or permission change.

cna.title: MISP CLI User Edit and Disable Do Not Invalidate Existing Open Sessions

ai_annotations.description: Draft vulnerability metadata was generated from a git-format patch using an Ollama-hosted language model. Human validation is required before publication.

assumptions: The session validation mechanism (AppController::__verifyUser) is assumed to check date_modified to decide whether to reload user state, as stated in the test file comments. This was not independently verified beyond the patch evidence.

The affected version range is assumed to be all MISP versions prior to 2.5.52, based on the explicit context fixed_version field. The affected_version field in context is '0' which is interpreted as 'all prior versions.'
CAPEC-66 (Session Fixation) is the closest available pattern but does not precisely describe 'session not invalidated after administrative disable.' The mapping is approximate.
CVSS PR:L assumes the affected user already has a valid authenticated session; the vulnerability does not grant new access but fails to revoke existing access.
The patch does not indicate whether other CLI operations (e.g., role changes via other commands) have the same issue; only the edit and disable paths in cli_users.php are addressed.
No explicit finder or reporter is identified in the patch metadata or commit message.

capecRationale.rationale: This is the closest available CAPEC pattern. The vulnerability involves a session persisting beyond its intended validity period because the invalidation trigger (date_modified update) was not fired. Strictly, CAPEC-66 describes an attacker fixing a session ID before authentication, which is not exactly this scenario. However, the underlying mechanism is the same: a session remains active when it should have been invalidated. No CAPEC pattern specifically covers 'session not invalidated after administrative disable,' so CAPEC-66 is selected as the best available match with acknowledged imprecision.

x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N: MISP is a network-accessible web application; sessions are maintained over the network. AC:L: The condition is straightforward - an admin disables a user via CLI while the user has an active session; no race condition or special timing is required. AT:N: No manipulation of an attack target is needed. PR:L: The affected party must already hold a valid authenticated session (low privilege - any authenticated user). UI:N: No victim interaction is required beyond the admin performing the CLI action. VC:N/VI:N: The user already had access before the disable; the issue is the failure to revoke, not a new data exposure. VA:L: The availability of the security control (user disable) is compromised for the duration of the existing session. SC:N/SI:N: No cross-scope impact. SA:L: The security authority (access control enforcement) is weakened because the disable action does not take effect on active sessions.
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The CLI user edit and disable operations now include the date_modified field in the save operation's field list, ensuring the modification timestamp is updated. This causes the application's session validation logic to detect the change and reload the user's state in all open sessions, immediately reflecting the disable or permission change.

modelComparison.selectionNotice: The selected result is closest to model consensus; this heuristic does not establish factual correctness and human review remains required.

x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: Two changes in app/Console/Command/CLIShell/cli_users.php: (1) In the __editUser method, the save field list was changed from $editableFields to array_merge($editableFields, ['date_modified']) so the timestamp is persisted on edit. (2) In the __deleteUser method, the save field list was changed from ['disabled'] to ['disabled', 'date_modified'] so the timestamp is persisted on disable. A new test file (app/Test/CLIShellUserSessionRefreshTest.php) was added with three unit tests verifying that date_modified is included in the field list for both edit and disable operations, and that the admin is not prompted for it.

This is a failure to enforce session expiration/invalidation upon a security-relevant state change.

descriptions.value:
MISP contains an authorization bypass in its tag attachment functionality. The endpoints responsible for editing event tags, editing attribute tags, and adding tags to event reports accepted arbitrary tag IDs without verifying whether the authenticated user was permitted to attach the referenced tag.

The events/addTag endpoint already resolved tag IDs through a restricted lookup that enforced per-user and per-organisation tag visibility rules. However, the three tag-editor endpoints (editEventTags, editAttributeTags, and eventReports/addTag) passed the supplied tag IDs directly to the attachment logic without any such check.

Preconditions:
- An authenticated user with tagger and add permissions on the target event/attribute/report.
- Knowledge or discovery of a tag ID that is restricted (local_only) to another organisation.

Impact:
- A user can attach a tag that is restricted to a different organisation, effectively bypassing the tag visibility and scoping model.
- A local_only tag can be attached as a global tag, violating the intended distribution restriction and potentially exposing the existence or semantics of another organisation's restricted tag to a broader audience.
- Data integrity of the MISP instance is compromised as the tag association model no longer reflects the intended access-control boundaries.

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52.
CAPEC-114 Parameter Tampering

solutions.value: The fix introduces a centralized authorization check that resolves the requested tag IDs against the user's permitted tag set before any attachment occurs. Each of the three previously vulnerable endpoints now queries the Tag model for the subset of requested IDs the user is allowed to attach, and filters out any IDs that fail the check. Additionally, the local_only flag is enforced so that a restricted tag cannot be attached as a global tag by a user who does not own it.

cna.title: MISP: Missing Authorization on Tag Attachment Endpoints Allows Attaching Restricted Tags by ID

ai_annotations.description: Draft vulnerability metadata was generated from a git-format patch using an Ollama-hosted language model. Human validation is required before publication.

assumptions: The affected version range is assumed to be all MISP versions prior to 2.5.52 based on the explicit context; the patch does not contain explicit version boundary markers.
PR:L assumes the attacker needs at minimum tagger and add permissions; the exact role requirements may vary by deployment configuration.
CAPEC-114 (Parameter Tampering) is the closest available pattern; a more specific IDOR-via-numeric-ID pattern is not present in the CAPEC catalog.

The CVSS VI:L and SI:L ratings assume the primary impact is data-model integrity (unauthorized tag associations) rather than full data exfiltration; if downstream consumers rely on tag scoping for access decisions, the effective impact could be higher.
The commit date is 2026-11-16; the fixed version 2.5.52 is taken from the analyst-supplied explicit context.

capecRationale.rationale: The attacker manipulates the tag_id parameter supplied to the tag-editor endpoints to reference a tag ID belonging to another organisation or a local_only tag, bypassing the intended access-control scoping. This is the closest CAPEC pattern: the parameter (tag ID) is valid in format but references a resource the user is not authorized to use. Uncertainty: CAPEC-114 is a broad pattern; a more specific 'IDOR via numeric ID' pattern does not exist in CAPEC, so this is the best available match.

x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N - MISP is a network-accessible web application. AC:L - The attacker only needs a valid tag ID (discoverable via enumeration or prior knowledge) and a standard API call; no race conditions or special timing required. AT:N - No attack-target manipulation needed. PR:L - Requires an authenticated user with tagger and add permissions. UI:N - No victim interaction required. VC:N - No direct confidentiality loss of system data; the tag name may be inferred but the primary issue is integrity. VI:L - Integrity impact is low: unauthorized tags are attached and local_only scoping is violated, but the core data store is not corrupted or deleted. VA:N - No availability impact. SC:N - No secondary confidentiality impact. SI:L - Secondary integrity: the tag association model is violated, potentially affecting downstream consumers of MISP data. SA:N - No secondary availability impact.
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The fix introduces a centralized authorization check that resolves the requested tag IDs against the user's permitted tag set before any attachment occurs. Each of the three previously vulnerable endpoints now queries the Tag model for the subset of requested IDs the user is allowed to attach, and filters out any IDs that fail the check. Additionally, the local_only flag is enforced so that a restricted tag cannot be attached as a global tag by a user who does not own it.

modelComparison.selectionNotice: The selected result is closest to model consensus; this heuristic does not establish factual correctness and human review remains required.

x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: A new method attachableTagIdsForUser() was added to the Tag model. It accepts a user array and a list of tag IDs, applies the existing createConditions() scoping (which enforces organisation and local_only restrictions), and returns a map of authorized tag IDs to their local_only flag. In AttributesController::editAttributeTags, EventsController::editEventTags, and EventReportsController::addTag, the requested tag ID lists are now filtered through this method before the attachment loop executes. IDs not present in the returned map are silently dropped (or rejected with an error in the event-reports path). A regression test class RestrictedTagAttachById was added to tests/testregressions.py verifying that restricted tags cannot be attached cross-organisation while open tags and own-organisation restricted tags still attach correctly.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The three tag-editor endpoints accepted and acted on arbitrary tag IDs without performing an authorization check to confirm the user was permitted to attach the specific tag. The events/addTag endpoint already had this check, but the other three paths did not, constituting a missing authorization control on a per-resource basis.

Even when a tag was visible to the user, the local_only scoping was not enforced in the editor endpoints, allowing a local_only tag to be attached as a global tag. This is an improper authorization decision regarding the scope of the tag attachment.

Operation Delegation SSRF protection bypass via DNS rebinding in Eclipse BaSyx Java Server SDK

descriptions.value: CAPEC-664 Server Side Request Forgery
CAPEC-275 DNS Rebinding

In Eclipse BaSyx Java Server SDK versions 2.0.0-milestone-10 to 2.0.0-milestone-16, the destination validation of the Operation Delegation feature, introduced to prevent server-side request forgery (CVE-2026-7412), can be bypassed through DNS rebinding.



Before dispatching a delegated Operation invocation, the server resolves the host of the `invocationDelegation` qualifier URI and rejects loopback, private, link-local, multicast and cloud metadata addresses. The outbound HTTP client (Reactor Netty), however, performs its own, independent DNS lookup when opening the connection and does not use the validated addresses. An attacker who can create or update a Submodel Operation and controls the DNS records of the delegation host can answer the validation lookup with a public address and the connection lookup with an internal address. No authentication is required when the authorization feature is not enabled.



Invoking the Operation then causes the BaSyx server to send HTTP POST requests to destinations the protection is meant to block, such as services in internal IT/OT networks, loopback-only interfaces, or cloud metadata endpoints. The server can be used to pivot into network segments that are not directly reachable by the attacker.



Only deployments with the Operation Delegation feature enabled are affected. The feature is enabled by default.



The issue is fixed in Eclipse BaSyx Java Server SDK 2.0.0-milestone-17.

descriptions.value:
MISP Collections retained a sharing group reference (sharing_group_id) even when the collection's distribution level was below 4 (i.e., not restricted to a sharing group). As a result, the sharing group name and UUID were displayed in the collection index and view endpoints to any user who could see the collection, regardless of whether that user was a member of the sharing group. Additionally, when collections were pushed to remote MISP servers, the sharing group data was included in the push payload even for collections not distributed to a sharing group, potentially leaking the group identity to remote systems.

Preconditions:
- An authenticated user with sufficient access to view the affected collection (e.g., a collection with distribution 0-3 that is publicly or broadly visible).
- The collection must have a stale sharing_group_id stored from a prior save.

Impact:
- Unauthorized disclosure of the sharing group name and UUID to users outside the group.
- Potential leakage of sharing group structure to remote MISP servers via the push mechanism.
- An attacker could enumerate sharing group names to identify targeting opportunities.

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52.
CAPEC-114 Client-side enforcement of server-side security

descriptions.description: CWE-200 Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

solutions.value: The fix enforces that a collection's sharing group reference is only retained and displayed when the distribution level is 4 (sharing group only). On save, the model layer now clears the sharing_group_id whenever distribution is not 4. The controller layer strips the SharingGroup association from index and view responses for non-distribution-4 collections. The push data collection routine omits SharingGroup data for non-distribution-4 collections. A database migration clears all pre-existing stale sharing_group_id values on collections with distribution below 4, eliminating already-leaked references.

cna.title: MISP Collections Expose Sharing Group Name to Users Outside the Group

ai_annotations.description: Draft vulnerability metadata was generated from a git-format patch using an Ollama-hosted language model. Human validation is required before publication.

assumptions: The affected version range is assumed to be all MISP versions prior to 2.5.52, based on the explicit context providing fixed_version 2.5.52 and affected_version 0.
The sharing group name is considered sensitive information; the actual sensitivity depends on the deployment context and the number of sharing groups in use.

The push leakage impact is assessed as not affecting subsequent systems (SC:N) because the remote server receiving the push is already a trusted peer in the MISP federation; however, this is an assumption.
CAPEC-114 is selected as the closest available pattern; no CAPEC specifically covers server-side output filtering failures based on authorization context, so this mapping is approximate.
PR:L assumes the attacker needs at least a basic authenticated user account with visibility of the affected collection; the exact role requirements depend on MISP's access control configuration.
The patch does not indicate whether the sharing group name is considered highly sensitive in all deployments; VC:L is chosen as a conservative assessment.

capecRationale.rationale: This is the closest available CAPEC pattern. The vulnerability involves server-side security enforcement (filtering sensitive data based on the user's authorization context) not being properly applied at the data-output layer. The sharing group data was included in responses without verifying the viewer's membership. CAPEC-114 is an imperfect match because the issue is server-side rather than client-side, but no CAPEC pattern specifically covers 'server-side information disclosure due to missing output filtering based on authorization context.' This is the best available mapping.

x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N - exploitable over the network via the MISP web API. AC:L - no special conditions; any user who can view the collection sees the sharing group name. AT:N - no attack target manipulation needed. PR:L - requires an authenticated user with access to view the collection. UI:N - no user interaction required; the data is returned in standard API responses. VC:L - low confidentiality impact: the sharing group name and UUID are disclosed, which is sensitive but limited in scope. VI:N, VA:N - no integrity or availability impact. SC:N, SI:N, SA:N - no subsequent system impact is evidenced; the push leakage is to a system the user already has a relationship with.
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The fix enforces that a collection's sharing group reference is only retained and displayed when the distribution level is 4 (sharing group only). On save, the model layer now clears the sharing_group_id whenever distribution is not 4. The controller layer strips the SharingGroup association from index and view responses for non-distribution-4 collections. The push data collection routine omits SharingGroup data for non-distribution-4 collections. A database migration clears all pre-existing stale sharing_group_id values on collections with distribution below 4, eliminating already-leaked references.

modelComparison.selectionNotice: The selected result is closest to model consensus; this heuristic does not establish factual correctness and human review remains required.

x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: CollectionsController.php: view() and index() now unset the SharingGroup association from the response data when Collection.distribution is not 4. Collection.php model: beforeValidate() clears sharing_group_id to null when distribution is not 4 (on create or when distribution is explicitly set); collectDataForPush() unsets SharingGroup from each row when distribution is not 4. A new migration (Migration_20261115_134841) runs an UPDATE to set sharing_group_id to NULL for all collections where distribution != 4 and sharing_group_id IS NOT NULL. Regression tests in PHP and Python verify that the sharing group is dropped on add/edit below dist 4, retained on dist 4, and not visible to non-members.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The sharing group name and UUID were exposed in API responses (index, view) and push payloads to users who were not members of the sharing group, constituting unauthorized information disclosure.

The display and push of the sharing group reference was not gated by a check that the requesting user is a member of the group or that the collection's distribution level warrants the association. The authorization logic (distribution level) was not enforced at the data-output layer.

Rapid7 Metasploit Framework versions prior to 6.5.10 are vulnerable to an uncontrolled resource consumption issue in Rex::Proto::Http::Request#normalize!. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can send an HTTP request with a deeply nested path that triggers repeated rescans of the request target, causing quadratic CPU consumption and temporarily degrading the availability of any affected HTTP listener.

cna.title: Incorrect authorization in embedded relation writes in Laravel MongoDB

descriptions.value: An incorrect authorization weakness in the embedded relation handling of the Laravel MongoDB library may allow a user with basic application privileges to alter records belonging to other users. After an embedded relation is pre-loaded, a routine write on that record is issued without the constraint that limits it to the record the user is permitted to change. This may result in unintended modification or loss of stored data for other users of the same application.

cna.title: Ever Gauzy: Deactivated user account retains full API access via JWT validation not re-checking isActive/isArchived

descriptions.value: Ever Gauzy is an open source business management platform for ERP, CRM, HRM, ATS, and project management. Prior to 111.44.3, per-request JWT validation in packages/core/src/lib/auth/strategies/jwt.strategy.ts accepts the result of UserService.getIfExists in packages/core/src/lib/user/user.service.ts without requiring User.isActive to be true and User.isArchived to be false. When a token contains an organizationId claim, the active and archived status check applies to the UserOrganization record rather than the User entity. After an administrator deactivates an account through PATCH /api/user/:id, an existing access token can continue to authenticate API requests at the account's previous privilege level until expiration, up to 24 hours by default. This issue is fixed in version 111.44.3.

MISP's LinOTPAuth plugin, used for one-time-password authentication against a LinOTP server, did not enforce TLS server certificate verification when the LinOTPAuth.verifyssl configuration option was not explicitly set. In a default or minimally configured deployment, the authentication request to the LinOTP server was sent without peer or peer-name certificate validation, effectively allowing self-signed or spoofed certificates.

An attacker with a network position between the MISP instance and the LinOTP server could perform a man-in-the-middle attack to intercept or tamper with the authentication exchange, potentially capturing one-time passwords or user credentials.

Preconditions:
- The LinOTPAuth plugin is enabled and configured to communicate with a LinOTP server
- The LinOTPAuth.verifyssl setting is absent or null (not explicitly set to true or false)
- The attacker can position themselves on the network path between MISP and the LinOTP server

Security impact:
- Confidentiality of OTP tokens and authentication credentials in transit
- Potential for credential interception or replay

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52
CAPEC-119 Man-in-the-Middle

solutions.value: The default behavior of the LinOTPAuth.verifyssl setting was changed so that a missing or null value now enables full TLS certificate verification (peer and peer-name validation). Only an explicit false value disables verification. This ensures that, by default, the MISP-to-LinOTP authentication channel is protected against man-in-the-middle attacks unless an administrator consciously opts out.
